currentAffairs.Category:

currentAffairs.Short_Summary:

currentAffairs.Full_Content:
WHAT HAPPENED ON THE FLYDUBAI AIRCRAFT

Syllabus areas:

GS Paper II – International Relations

GS Paper III – Internal Security

Flight Diverted After In-Flight Pilot Assault

On September 30, 2026, at around 8:35 a.m. IST, a flydubai flight travelling from the United Arab Emirates to Israel was diverted to Saudi Arabia following a serious in-flight incident involving its pilots.

The incident occurred aboard Boeing 737-8 MAX flight FZ 1073, which was carrying predominantly Israeli passengers. One pilot reportedly stabbed the other and allegedly attempted to crash the aircraft. The flight was subsequently diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely despite sustaining significant damage.

Following the incident, fly Dubai announced the suspension of all flights to and from Israel. Authorities have launched an investigation into the incident, including examination of a possible terrorism-related motive.

What happened on the flight?

According to media reports, an altercation reportedly broke out between the two flight crew members during the journey, resulting in one pilot being stabbed. The captain, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national and former SpiceJet pilot, had joined flydubai in 2022. The co-pilot, who was reportedly arrested following the incident, has been identified in media reports as an Omani national. Both crew members were subsequently shifted to Abu Dhabi after receiving initial medical treatment in Saudi Arabia.

Media reports, eyewitness accounts and videos recorded during the flight indicate that passengers were caught amid considerable confusion and panic, particularly near the front section of the aircraft.

According to reports by Reuters and The Times of Israel, citing a spokesperson for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the injured captain reportedly managed to open the cockpit door after being attacked. This enabled several Israeli passengers to enter the cockpit and restrain the alleged attacker. Other flydubai pilots who were present in the passenger cabin reportedly intervened and helped ensure that the aircraft landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

Weapon Used and Condition of the Crew

Initial accounts from passengers suggested that a pocket knife may have been used during the attack, while other reports indicated that the aircraft’s flight-deck crash axe could have been involved. However, a BBC report on October 3, citing the United Arab Emirates Prosecutor General, stated that the pilot was attacked with a crash axe in an alleged attempt to take control of the aircraft.

Senior pilots told The Hindu that a crash axe is a mandatory emergency safety tool carried for use by flight crew. It is generally kept in the flight deck in an easily accessible location and may be used during emergencies, including breaching the fuselage when structural deformation occurs or opening panels to access the source of smoke or fire.

A video shared with The Hindu by aviation sources reportedly showed both pilots on the cabin floor with serious bleeding and bloodstains visible on the cabin wall. One pilot appeared to be wearing a blood-soaked uniform with epaulettes, while the other was seen using an oxygen mask. Several passengers near the injured crew members were reportedly heard asking that the incident not be filmed.

What happened to the flight?

Amid the chaos in the flight deck, the aircraft transmitted a series of transponder codes, internationally recognised signals used to indicate emergencies during flight. In this case, codes 7700 and 7500 indicated a general emergency and possible unlawful interference, respectively. The signals may have prompted Israel and Saudi Arabia to deploy fighter aircraft in response.

At around 10:50 a.m. IST, the Boeing, which was cruising at approximately 34,000 feet, suddenly descended to nearly 19,000 feet. The aircraft subsequently climbed and descended again before stabilising at around 15,000 feet.

The incident occurred approximately two-and-a-half hours into the three-hour journey. After briefly entering Jordanian airspace, the aircraft turned back towards Saudi Arabia and eventually landed safely at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk. The airport is a civil-military facility and also serves as a base for Royal Saudi Air Force Wing 7.

Aircraft Damage and Emergency Landing

An emergency descent can be carried out in a controlled manner. However, if the descent is erratic or uncontrolled, it can place significant stress on critical flight-control surfaces and potentially cause structural damage, including to the aircraft’s tail section.

Images taken on the ground at Tabuk reportedly showed substantial damage to the aircraft’s rudder and vertical stabiliser, with a large portion of the structure appearing to be missing. Passengers were seen disembarking from the aircraft using a step ladder operated by Saudi Ground Services Company, the airport’s ground-handling agency.

The airport authorities stated that their Air Traffic Control (ATC) centre received a distress call from the aircraft, in which the crew requested permission for an emergency landing.

What Has the Airline Said?

In statements shared with The Hindu, a flydubai spokesperson confirmed that an altercation had occurred in the flight deck during the flight. The spokesperson stated that the aircraft was subsequently secured by off-duty flydubai crew members travelling on the same flight, who intervened, diverted the aircraft and successfully landed it with all 172 passengers and crew members safe.

The airline said that the reasons and motives behind the incident remain unknown and are subject to a formal investigation. It urged all parties to avoid premature conclusions or speculation while authorities continue to establish the facts.

Flydubai also announced that all flights to and from Israel would remain suspended while the investigation into the incident is underway.

How Is the Investigation Proceeding?

Authorities have initiated a formal investigation into the incident, while aviation experts have drawn comparisons with previous cases involving suspected unlawful interference or deliberate actions by flight crew.

Earlier incidents of this nature include Japan Airlines Flight 350 (1982), Royal Air Maroc Flight 630 (1994), SilkAir Flight 185 (1997), EgyptAir Flight 990 (1999), LAM Mozambique Airlines Flight 470 (2013), and Germanwings Flight 9525 (2015).

In response to the incident, Israel has decided to strengthen security screening procedures for pilots operating flights into the country, as authorities examine the circumstances and possible motives behind the incident.

currentAffairs.Short_Summary: The article highlights how women and transgender persons are transforming Swachhata into a pathway for livelihoods, dignity and social inclusion. currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Beyond Cleanliness: The Women and Transgender Changemakers of Swachhata

Syllabus areas:

Essay

GS Paper II – Governance & Social Justice

GS Paper III – Environment & Sustainable Development

GS Paper I – Indian Society

GS Paper IV – Ethics, Integrity & Aptitude

A clean city is often defined by what is no longer visible—waste on streets, blocked drains and inadequate sanitation. Behind this transformation are women turning waste into livelihoods and transgender persons gaining professional roles in sanitation. Swachhata Hi Seva 2026 promotes this spirit through citizen participation, dignity, enterprise and collective responsibility towards a Swachh and Viksit Bharat.

When waste become a livelihood:

Around gaushalas and dairies, cow dung can become a waste-management challenge, especially when it enters drains and sewage channels. In Krishna Vihar Colony, Loni, Uttar Pradesh, a group of women found an innovative solution by using cow dung to make incense sticks and Loban cups. What began with 8–10 women gradually became a livelihood opportunity for many more.

A woman from the Loni Nagar Palika Parishad supported the initiative by connecting the producers with gaushala owners for a steady supply and effective utilisation of cow dung. During the summer, when demand for incense products peaks, the initiative employs around 40–50 women, providing livelihood, dignity and economic opportunity. The Nagar Palika Parishad also earns up to 25% revenue from product sales.

The products use around 30–35% dry cow-dung powder, reducing the requirement for wood sawdust and promoting reuse. They are supplied across India, including Delhi, Mumbai, Punjab, Gujarat and Hyderabad, and have also reached Mauritius and South Africa.

The initiative is now exploring cow-dung fuel for cremation grounds and havans, along with biodegradable flower pots that can return to the soil as manure. Thus, waste is transformed into livelihood, enterprise and environmental value.

From waste collectors to waste leaders:

In Patna, Bihar, women are breaking traditional conventions and giving cleanliness an inclusive dimension. At the city's Pink Material Recovery Facility (MRF), women play a central role in waste management under a female supervisor. The facility processes dry and wet waste, handling around 2 tonnes of dry waste and 1.5 tonnes of wet waste daily.

The Pink MRF was established to create employment opportunities for women in waste management. Patna Municipal Corporation supported the initiative, enabling the facility to be set up within three months. Through the ‘Cash for Waste’ initiative, citizens can bring dry waste and receive payment, creating incentives for community participation while giving waste economic value.

Patna has also transformed old, unusable vehicles into mobile Pink Toilets, demonstrating the principles of the 3Rs—Reduce, Reuse and Recycle. Together, these initiatives link sanitation with women's empowerment, environmental sustainability, community participation and livelihood opportunities, showing how inclusive participation can strengthen urban cleanliness.

Women who carry cleanliness into their communities:

Women are transforming Swachhata by strengthening community participation. In Bhopal, 250 women brand ambassadors support cleanliness and waste management, while ‘Bartan Banks’ across 25 wards promote reusable utensils and reduce single-use plastic. A 60-member ‘Swachhata Kitty Group’ contributes monthly towards community cleanliness activities.

In Uttarakhand, the ‘Bainni Sena’, comprising 570 women across 57 groups, monitors cleanliness, spreads awareness and connects citizens with municipal authorities. In Shillong, the Lynnehskhem Self-Help Group collects wet waste and converts biodegradable waste into compost, creating livelihoods through rehabilitation and training. Together, these initiatives turn Swachhata into a shared culture of care, participation and sustainability.

When Inclusion Changes the Face of Sanitation:

In Odisha, transgender persons are gaining professional roles at the heart of urban sanitation systems. The initiative began in Cuttack, where the Municipal Corporation formed a transgender Self-Help Group, provided training and entrusted its members with operating and maintaining a Septage Treatment Plant. The model later expanded across Odisha, with Urban Local Bodies partnering with Self-Help Groups in Faecal Sludge and Septage Management (FSSM) and solid waste management.

In Bhubaneswar, the Swikruti Self-Help Group operates and maintains a 75-KLD Faecal Sludge Treatment Plant (FSTP) at Basuaghai after receiving technical and managerial training. The initiative has strengthened professional identity, confidence and social recognition among members. The Bhubaneswar Municipal Corporation has also involved transgender groups in operating seven cesspool vehicles, with minimum applicable wages and training in health, hygiene, personal protective equipment and desludging protocols. Odisha's initiative demonstrates how inclusive livelihoods can advance both sanitation and social empowerment.

The Deeper Meaning of Swachhata:

These stories show that Swachhata can do more than create cleaner surroundings. It can open doors to livelihoods,participation, and recognition. The real transformation lies not only in what happens to waste, but in what becomes possible for the people who manage it. When people once pushed to the margins find a place at the heart Of Swachhata, cleanliness takes on a deeper meaning. It becomes a shared effort, shaped by dignity, opportunity and a sense of belonging.

Essay
currentAffairs.Short_Summary:
The article explores how unpaid household and care work, often overlooked in economic statistics, contributes significantly to human capital, family welfare and the wider economy.

It highlights the Supreme Court’s recognition of “loss of domestic care” as a distinct compensable contribution, marking a shift from “invisible work” to measurable economic value.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
From “Invisible Work” to “Measurable Work”

Syllabus areas:

GS Paper I – Indian Society

GS Paper II – Social Justice

GS Paper III – Indian Economy

GS Paper IV – Ethics

Essay

The SC on June 11, 2026 held that unpaid domestic labour performed by Housewives must be assigned an independent economic value while determining compensation in motor accident death cases, they are accidents involving motor vehicles—such as cars, buses, trucks, motorcycles, or autorickshaws—that cause injury, death, or property damage. It fixed minimum notional income 30000 per month.

Home makers are Nation builders.

Care work includes childcare, elderly care, supporting persons with disabilities, nutrition, health management and emotional support within households. Though often unpaid and invisible in economic statistics, it directly contributes to human capital formation by improving health, education, skills and productivity.

Well-nourished and adequately cared-for children are more likely to develop better cognitive and physical capabilities, perform well in education and become productive members of the workforce. Similarly, care for elderly and dependent persons supports the well-being of the entire household.

Thus, unpaid care work creates a social and economic foundation for future productivity. Recognising, reducing and redistributing this work through childcare facilities, healthcare services, social protection and greater sharing of household responsibilities can strengthen both human capital and inclusive economic growth.

Created distinct head of compensation called "loss of domestic care" in motor accident claims and mandated a 10% increase in this amount every three years.

The ruling came in an appeal from a motor accident claim in Punjab.

Observing that welfare-oriented objective of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, India’s principal legislation regulating motor vehicles, road transport and traffic. It covers vehicle registration, driving licences, permits, insurance, road safety, offences, penalties and compensation for victims of motor accidents, is frustrated when compensation claims remain pending for years.

SC says – Cooking, cleaning, caregiving etc play vital role in contribution of GDP.

Therefore, Home makers are architects of India's human capital. It recognised unpaid domestic work as a measurable economic contribution.

Methods of Valuing Unpaid Domestic Work:

Unpaid domestic work can be valued through three major methods: Replacement Cost Method, which estimates the cost of hiring workers for similar services; Opportunity Cost Method, based on income forgone by the homemaker; and Output Method, which estimates the monetary value of goods and services produced within the household.

Court noted that women spend over seven hours a day on unpaid domestic tasks, nearly 2.6 times more unpaid caregiving work than men and contribute an estimated 15–17% of India's GDP through this labour. That figure appears nowhere in the national accounts. Conventional GDP measurement excludes household production entirely.

For the life insurance industry, the ruling is an instruction it should act on without waiting for a regulatory directive. The Court limited the home maker definition to women only; if a man does the same, what next? and an unemployed job seeker between placements or yet to enter employment these are also "non-earning woman performing domestic work".

Constitutional Linkages with Homemakers:

Constitutional ArticleLink with Homemakers
Article 14Recognition of homemakers' unpaid work supports equality before law and equal treatment in compensation and social protection.
Article 15Addresses gender-based disadvantages arising from the traditional unequal distribution of domestic and care responsibilities.
Article 16Unequal household responsibilities can affect women's access to education, employment and opportunities for economic participation.
Article 21Recognition of domestic work reinforces the dignity, autonomy and value of homemakers' contributions to family and society.
Article 39(a)Homemakers contribute significantly to the family's livelihood and economic well-being through unpaid domestic and care work.
Article 39(d)Raises the broader issue of recognising and fairly valuing work traditionally performed by women without monetary remuneration.
Article 42Supports the need for humane conditions for women, maternity relief, childcare and institutional support for care responsibilities.
Article 43Connects with the broader objective of ensuring decent living conditions and economic security for women and care workers.

Unpaid Work and Female Labour Force Participation:

The unequal burden of unpaid domestic and caregiving work can constrain women’s participation in the formal labour market. Time spent on cooking, cleaning, childcare and elderly care reduces the time available for paid employment, education and skill development. This can contribute to career interruptions, lower earnings and economic dependence. Improving access to childcare, healthcare, sanitation, water supply, safe transport and flexible work arrangements can reduce this burden and enable greater workforce participation. Thus, recognising and redistributing unpaid work is important for women’s economic empowerment, inclusive growth and human capital development.

currentAffairs.Category: UPSC
currentAffairs.Short_Summary:
The article traces the 100-year institutional journey of the UPSC, from its establishment in 1926 to its present status as an independent constitutional body.
It highlights the Commission’s role in recruitment, examinations, government advice and public-service administration, and its contribution to nation-building over a century.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
UPSC at 100: A Century of Public Service and Nation-Building

On 1 October 2026, the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) completes one hundred years. Its institutional journey began on 1 October 1926, when India’s first Public Service Commission was constituted - an advisory body whose Chairman and Members were appointed by the Secretary of State in London. Over the century that followed, the Commission evolved in structure, status and responsibilities, becoming what it is today - an independent constitutional body.

The Road to 1926

The principle that entry into public service should rest on merit rather than patronage took formal shape in 1855, when the Indian Civil Service (ICS) examination was instituted in London, replacing the East India Company’s system of nomination with open competition. For most Indians, however, the door remained nearly impossible to open. The examination was held only in London, in English, and tested candidates on subjects such as Greek and Latin - not because these were needed to govern a district in Bengal or Punjab, but because they favoured those educated in the British system.

In 1862, 21-year-old Satyendranath Tagore, elder brother of Rabindranath Tagore, sailed from Calcutta to England to sit an examination his own country would not let him take at home. He cleared it in 1863 and joined the service in 1864 - the first Indian in what the British called the “heaven-born service”. He served for over thirty years in the Bombay Presidency. Six years after his success, Surendranath Banerjee, Behari Lal Gupta and Romesh Chunder Dutt followed. The maximum age for the examination was, however, progressively reduced from 23 to 19, leaving Indian candidates little time to prepare. By 1919, only 78 of the 1,255 ICS officers were Indian.

Sustained nationalist demands brought gradual change. The Government of India Act, 1919, enacted after the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, provided for a Public Service Commission. In 1922, the ICS examination was held in India for the first time, at Allahabad, alongside London. In 1928 the Indian centre moved to Delhi. In 1924, the Lee Commission, chaired by Arthur Hamilton Lee, recommended the immediate establishment of a statutory Public Service Commission. It also proposed that of every ten new entrants, four would be British, four Indian and two Indians promoted from the provincial services - on paper a path to parity, in practice a guaranteed 40 per cent of every intake for the British, by birth rather than by competition.

The Commission was established under the Public Service Commission (Functions) Rules, 1926, framed under Sections 96B and 96C of the 1919 Act. Sir Ross Barker, a member of the Home Civil Service of the United Kingdom, was its first Chairman, assisted by four Members, and the Commission was housed at Metcalfe House, Delhi. Its limited powers drew sustained criticism from leaders of the freedom movement. Yet a permanent recruiting body now existed in India, seated and staffed in India - which is why the Commission dates its history from 1926.

The Constitutional Mandate

On 22 August 1949, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, Chairman of the Drafting Committee, moved the draft articles on the Union and State Public Service Commissions in the Constituent Assembly. They became Part XIV (Articles 315–323) of the Constitution. In his valedictory address on 26 November 1949, Dr. Rajendra Prasad emphasised that the independence of the Public Service Commissions was essential to ensure impartiality in public appointments and to guard against jobbery, nepotism and favouritism.

ArticleWhat it provides
315Public Service Commissions for the Union and for the States, with provision for a Joint Commission for two or more States
316Chairman and Members appointed by the President
317Removal or suspension of a Member only by order of the President, after an inquiry by the Supreme Court
318Power to make regulations on the conditions of service of Members and staff
319Restrictions on holding office after ceasing to be a Member; the Chairman is ineligible for further employment under the Government of India or a State
320Functions: conducting examinations for appointment to the services of the Union, and advising on methods of recruitment, promotions and disciplinary matters
321Power of Parliament or a State Legislature to extend the Commission’s functions
322Expenses of the Commission charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
323Annual report to the President; cases where the Commission’s advice was not accepted, with reasons, laid before Parliament

currentAffairs.Title: Nerve Agents
currentAffairs.Category: GS Paper III – Science & Technology, Internal Security, Disaster Management
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: Nerve agents are highly toxic chemical warfare agents that disrupt the nervous system by interfering with acetylcholine regulation. The article examines their mechanism, major types, health effects, international controls and challenges in preventing chemical-weapons misuse.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Nerve Agents

Syllabus areas:

GS Paper III – Science & Technology, Internal Security, Disaster Management

Nerve agent is a highly toxic chemical that disrupts nervous system in the human body by blocking acetylcholinesterase, an enzyme needed for normal nerve and muscle function.

Nerve agents can be absorbed by inhalation, ingestion or contact with skin or eyes.

Nerve agents block acetylcholinesterase, an enzyme needed for nerve signalling, causing muscle twitching, breathing difficulty, paralysis and death.

Examples of major nerve agents:

  • Tabun (GA)
  • Sarin (GB)
  • Soman (GD)
  • VX

    • Nerve agents are first time discovered by German Scientists while developing insecticides. In 1930s, German chemists studying organo phosphate insecticides discovered compounds such as tabun and sarin that were extremely toxic to nervous system.

    therefore Tabun – is the first nerve agent discovered in 1936 in Germany.

    Sarin – A fast acting nerve agent that evaporates quickly and is mainly inhaled.

    Soman – More persistent than sarin and harder to treat after exposure.

    VX – An oily nerve agent that can remain on surfaces for long periods and be absorbed through skin.

    A-series agents such as A-232, A-234 which are commonly discussed as Novichok agents.

    All these nerve agents are prohibited chemical weapons under Chemical Weapons Convention. These are classified as Schedule 1 chemicals, meaning their permitted uses are extremely limited to purposes such as research, medical, pharma, agriculture under Controls.

    There are also other chemical warfare agents such as mustard agents and certain choking agents but these belong to different chemical classes and act differently from nerve agents.

    Chemical warfare means using toxic chemicals as weapons to kill, injure, incapacitate, or otherwise harm people or animals during armed conflict.

    Examples include:

  • Nerve agents: Sarin, tabun, Soman, VX.
  • Blister agents: Sulfur mustard
  • Choking agents: Chlorine, phosgene
  • Blood agents: Hydrogen cyanide

    • Chemical Weapons Convention prohibits development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons.

    Brief History of Nerve agents

  • Germany – 1930s – the first known nerve agent, tabun was discovered (1936) Sarin (1938) Soman (1944)
  • World War II – Germany produced and stockpiled nerve agents, but they were not used in battlefield.
  • British Researchers developed the compound that is VX.
  • Cold War – USA, USSR maintained substantial chemical weapons programs.
  • Halabja chemical attack in Iraq in 1988, killed thousands.
  • Iran-Iraq war (1980's) – Iraqi forces used chemical weapons.
  • Tokyo subway attack – 1995 – Members of Aum Shinrikyo cult released sarin gas in the Tokyo subway, killing 13 people and injuring thousands.
  • Syria (2013-2017) – investigations linked multiple attacks involving sarin to Syrian Civil War
  • Sergei Skripal Poisoning – 2018 – Former Russian spy Sergei Skripal and his daughter were poisoned in UK with a Novichok nerve agent.

    • Detecting Nerve agents in the Human Body

    Nerve agents can be detected in the body, but they are often broken down rapidly, so testing is time-sensitive. Blood tests, urine tests, environmental sample tests etc are available.

    Now Indian scientists have found a solution: Nano-material that can detect and neutralise nerve agents within 13 seconds.

    They developed cerium based nanozyme, a material engineered to behave like a natural enzyme, that reacts quickly with organophosphate compounds (nerve agents).

    Cerium is the most abundant rare-earth metal and helps create the bright white light in energy saving bulbs and LEDs.

    Interesting point is that – this nanozyme is designed for on-site detection of contamination, not for medical or blood testing. It can be used to identify toxic residues on surfaces, equipment, or in industrial and environmental settings – situation where rapid, reliable detection is critical.

currentAffairs.Title: AI-NOMICS
currentAffairs.Category: GS Paper III – Science & Technology, Economy, Internal Security
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: The article explores how AI is transforming economic activity through tokenisation, AI-driven productivity, digital finance and emerging business models. It examines the growing economic significance of AI, including its impact on markets, jobs, investment, innovation and financial systems.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
AI-NOMICS

Syllabus areas:

GS Paper III – Science & Technology, Economy, Internal Security

TOKENS – TOKENOMICS – TOKENISATION:

As humans, the smallest unit of information we use to represent language is a single character – i.e. a letter or a number or punctuation mark. But the smallest unit of language that a Large Language Model (LLM) uses is called a Token.

A token can be a set of characters or part of word or syllable or whole word or even a short multi word phrase. The code that converts language to tokens is called Tokeniser.

We may say that a token is about 2/3 to 3/4 of a word. But – image/audio/video-based inputs, it is not possible. Hence Token is defined in terms of "syllablesete". An english word is represented by approximately 1–5 tokens. If you input a prompt of 100 word long, the LLM will likely work with 150 tokens.

After the input is tokenised, the model then converts tokens into vectors which are long list of numbers. These vectors form the basic computational unit on which the model performs calculations to generate output.

TOKENOMICS: When it comes to LLMs, model providers such as OpenAI and the Anthropic bill customers by tokens, which directly relate to the amount of processing their GPUs (Graphic Processing Unit) perform for a given prompt.

Higher the tokens involved, higher the workload on GPU which in turn translate to higher cost for the model provider.

This billing by tokens is more true of enterprise customers who use APIs (Application Programming Interface) to connect their enterprise software to an LLM than of consumers like you and me.

Just as electricity bills are based on units consumed, LLM billing is based on tokens consumed. Electricity bills charge based on what kind of – industrial and residential. Similarly, pricing of LLMs depends on the complexity of the model. A larger, more robust model will cost more per token and vice-versa.

Typically, users are billed per million tokens and further, there is a difference based on whether token is part of the input or part of the output. Input tokens cost lower than output- tokens because the amount of processing required to generate a text output, for instance, is higher than reading a text input.

Over the past years, companies have pushed their workforce to adopt AI in their work flows, often without capping token consumption. Employees were even tracked and ranked based on token usage, as a proxy to measure productivity and to evaluate whether they have become “AI-Native”. This led to phenomenon known as Token maxxing.

Agentic AI:

Agentic AI is one of the most powerful applications of LLM. It refers to the ability of an AI model to spawn and deploy agents meant to carry out a complex task.

Here is how an Agent is defined:

“Agents are autonomous systems that can operate independently, use various tools to accomplish complex tasks, planned and executed step after step using the reasoning abilities of an LLM.”

Autonomy, ability to plan and reason, ability to handle complex tasks – all are defining characteristics of an agent. Another key feature of an agent is Ability to call the right tool to discharge the task.

Proprietary vs. Open-source models

A proprietary LLM is developed and owned by organisation that develops it. Everything is private and not available for access by outsiders.

Popular LLMs such as:

1. Open AI’s GPT series

2. Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet → Proprietary models

3. Google’s Gemini

Open source Model is available for commercial use by persons other than the developer

1. Deepseek – R1

2. Alibaba’s Qwen 3.6 → Open source models.

3. Meta’s Llama 4

In the traditional sense, open-source would mean that the source code is accessible.

Artificial General Intelligence AGI is when an AI system can match or surpass cognitive abilities of humans.

When that happens, AGI can autonomously learn, reason and transfer knowledge seamlessly from one unfamiliar task to another without human intervention. ∴ AGI is also referred to as strong AI

Artificial Narrow Intelligence ANI for only single and predefined task.

1. A chess bot

2. Facial Recognition software

3. Classifying emails spam

These cannot write essay or generate images or process medical scan.

∴ ANI is also referred to as weak AI

Today's LLMs are still technically ANI but just more. ∴ Between AGI and ANI, we have LLMs.

In Simple Terms:

Tokenisation is the process of breaking text into smaller pieces that an AI model can process. Tokens are the resulting pieces.

For ex: consider the sentence - "Artificial Intelligence is amazing" A tokeniser might split it into tokens like:  "Artificial"  "Intelligence"  "is"  "amazing"

or depending on the tokeniser, a long word may be split into subword tokens:

 "Art"  "ificial"  "intelligence"  "is"  "Amazing"

Modern AI models such as GPT models often use sub word tokenisation, where common words are single tokens but rare or long words are split into smaller parts. This allows the model to handle virtually any text efficiently.

Tokenisation:

∴ Tokenisation is the process and Tokens are the output of that process. Without tokenisation, language models cannot convert human-readable text into a form they can process.

Tokenisation:

Tokenisation is the creation, issuance or representation of assets on a digital token ledger or a programmable platform.

Tokenisation is linked to block chain technology. It came into prominence following the rise of cryptocurrencies.

All the transactions in the tokens are recorded on digital ledgers, which are transparent, secure and can be accessed by everyone.

Tokenisation is adopted in various countries.

The idea of converting all securities — equities, bonds, derivatives — into tokens and enabling trading and settlement through distributed ledger is good, since it is faster and lowers the intermediation cost, improves liquidity.

While many countries are weighing tokenisation, 91% of them have very limited or no tokenisation use cases, still in pilot phase. Only 11% of institutional investors have invested in tokenisation in 2025, 61% expecting to invest by 2026 end.

Real-World Assets (RWAs)

Real World Assets are physical or traditional financial assets such as real estate, commodities, bonds, stocks, and invoices that have intrinsic value in the real economy.

In this, tokenisation is the process of representing ownership or rights to these assets as digital tokens on a block chain.

While RWAs are the underlying assets, tokenisation is the technology that digitises them. This enables fractional ownership, improved liquidity, faster transactions and enhanced transparency.

currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Beyond the Label: Food Safety, Celebrity Endorsements and the Fight for Consumer Health

Syllabus areas:

GS Paper II: Governance

GS Paper III: Economy

GS Paper IV: Ethics

In an important intervention for promoting nutrition literacy, the Supreme Court of India strongly criticised the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) over prolonged delays in mandating front-of-pack warning labels (FOPL) for packaged foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fat. Hearing a public interest litigation by the NGO J3S and Our Health Society, Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran had rebuked the regulator, remarking, “If you can’t do it, we will,” and questioned the industry pressure facing the FSSAI. The Court tied food safety directly to Article 21 (right to health flowing from right to life) and Article 47 (State’s duty to improve public health), citing the severe rise in diseases like diabetes and childhood obesity.

The FSSAI had initially adopted a lenient stance, stating that warning labels would be required only when the marketed food products were deemed to have high levels of two or more of the nutrients sugar, salt and saturated fat, which should not be consumed in excess. The petitioners rightly argued that this would let off the hook products that are excessively high in only one of these nutrients, as they would still pose a health risk. This position was supported by Indian and global experts as well as the National Institute of Nutrition, which is part of the Indian Council of Medical Research. The court agreed with the petitioners and directed FSSAI to modify its stance on the FOPL warnings.

In another victory for the consumers’ right to be protected against misleading advertisements, the Delhi High Court recently rejected a plea by the makers of Vimal Elaichi to quash a show-cause notice issued to their brand ambassadors Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn and Tiger Shroff by the Food and Drugs Administration (FDA) of Maharashtra. The FDA alleged misrepresentation of the product, amounting to be a surrogate for the pan masala product which is sold in the state.

The Maharashtra FDA directed the actors to immediately cease appearing in the campaign and remove all related promotional material from their personal social media platform. The stars were given 15 days to hand over evidence of endorsement contracts and evidence of the due diligence they had conducted before signing the deal. The FDA directed the actors to immediately cease appearing in the campaign and remove all related promotional material from their personal social media platforms.

FSSAI had also earlier stated that it would introduce the warnings in two phases, with the single-nutrient warning label after providing sufficient time for the industry to re-formulate its products. That would mean the products sold in the markets with harmful levels of a single nutrient would carry no warnings to the consumer for a long time. Following the court’s stern directive, the FSSAI submitted that it would proceed with single-phase enforcement where warnings will apply immediately if any single of the critical nutrient crosses the defined high limit, rather than rolling out in delayed stages. Any food or beverage containing non-caloric sweeteners must explicitly display the front-of-pack statement: “Contains non-caloric sweetener”.

The FSSAI sought a four-month window to finalise draft regulations, followed by a voluntary implementation period of 365 days for businesses to exhaust existing packaging stock. On September 28, the Supreme Court asked why such a long time was needed for voluntary compliance and fresh stakeholder consultation given that the process had begun in 2022.

In August this year, the FSSAI too issued a countrywide warning to content creators, social media influencers and celebrities to desist from endorsing food products with unverified, exaggerated or scientifically-unproven health claims. As food products are being marketed with claims such as “boosts immunity” or “aids weight loss”, such a warning is timely.

During the 72nd National Film Awards in late September, President Droupadi Murmu urged the Indian film community to refrain from endorsing substances and ultra-processed products that damage public health, stating that a “true star spreads light, not darkness”. This advice, from India’s first citizen, must be heeded. The government’s chief economic advisor has also been drawing attention to unhealthy food products adversely impacting people’s health with consequent economic impact.

The behaviours of daily living extend from the diets and physical activity to sleep patterns and consumption of addictive substances like tobacco and alcohol. These behaviours affect many aspects of health and well-being. The alarming rise of chronic non-communicable diseases — such as cardiovascular diseases, cancers, diabetes and obesity—is mainly driven by unhealthy behaviour.

Health behaviours are usually steered by health beliefs that are based on information gathered from many sources, only some of which are reliable in terms of accuracy. Today’s behaviours, like diet and exercise, determine tomorrow’s risk factors, like obesity and high blood pressure. Today’s risk factors lead up to tomorrow’s diseases which can cause death or disability, so it is essential that people’s health beliefs and behaviours are guided by accurate and undistorted information on the basis of which they can protect, preserve and promote health of their families.

Elephant Deaths

Syllabus areas:

GS Paper III – Environment and Ecology

Human-induced elephant deaths are back in focus in Kerala after the death of a makhna (tuskless male) elephant reportedly after chewing on fruit stuffed with explosives, in the Malayattoor forests in Ernakulam district, Kerala.

This is the continuing elephant killings in Munnar – Pambikulam - Malayattor forest sector, one of the major elephant mortality hotspots in Kerala.

Crop raiding and habitat intrusion by elephants and retaliation by humans have contributed to elephant deaths.

Electrocution is the leading unnatural cause of death, with incident rates tripling over six years.

Explosives and poaching persist as threats, with juveniles 744 wild elephants died between April 2019 and March 2025, while human-induced causes accounted for 77 deaths. Munnar and Ranni areas accounted for the highest incidence of electrocution.

The primary elephant mortality zones in the State also included the wayanad landscape, Nilambur region and the Periyar – Ranni–Konni landscape.

· Orange: Wayanad landscape (Northern Kerala)

· Purple: Nilambur region (North-central Kerala)

· Blue/Teal: Periyar–Ranni–Konni landscape (Central and southeastern Kerala)

The death of a pregnant wild elephant in the Silent Valley forest in 2020, after feeding on fruit stuffed with firecrackers. The animal was unable to eat after feeding on the fruit and suffering injuries to its mouth, the animal had stayed in a river in an apparent effort to ease pain.

Recent visit of Donald Trump to China.

currentAffairs.Full_Content:
The Houthis and the Red Sea Crisis: Regional Conflict, Maritime Security and Implications for India

Syllabus areas:

GS Paper II – International Relations, Internal Security

GS Paper III – Indian Economy

Where: Yemen

Who: Leader — Abdul-Malik al-Houthi

What: Theme

  • Maintain and expand their political and military control in Yemen.
  • Oppose US and Israeli influence in the region.
  • Promote their Zaydi Islamic political ideology.
  • Support the Palestinian cause, which they use to support attacks on Israeli-linked targets and justify attacks on Red Sea shipping.
  • Resist Saudi Arabia and other regional forces opposing them.

    • Formal/Official Name: Ansar Allah

    Belong to: Yemen’s Zaydi Shia community

    Territorial Control: Sana’a, the capital of Yemen; significant parts of North and West Yemen.

    Supported by: Iran, which provides weapons, training, intelligence and technical expertise.

    Military Assistance: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Hezbollah.

    International Significance: Houthi forces have attacked ships in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, saying their actions are connected to the Israel–Gaza conflict.

    Why are they fighting?

    1. Yemen’s civil conflict: The Houthis fought Yemen’s internationally recognized government and its allies, including Saudi Arabia.

    2. Saudi Arabia: Saudi Arabia intervened militarily in Yemen because it viewed the Houthi takeover as a major security threat.

    3. Israel and Gaza: After the Israel–Hamas war began in October 2023, the Houthis began attacking ships they said were connected to Israel, claiming they were supporting Palestinians in Gaza.

    4. United States and other countries: Houthi attacks on shipping led the US, UK and other countries to conduct military operations against Houthi targets and deploy naval forces to protect shipping.

    Groups Associated with the Conflict

    These groups are often described collectively as part of Iran’s Axis of Resistance.

    Houthis vs. Red Sea — Crisis and Conflict

    Following the outbreak of the Israel–Hamas war in October 2023, the Houthis began attacking ships in and around the Red Sea.

    They said their attacks were intended to pressure Israel and support Palestinians.

    The attacks are against commercial shipping.

    The International Maritime Organization has condemned attacks on international shipping.

    The Red Sea is a major international shipping corridor connecting the Indian Ocean with the Mediterranean Sea through the Suez Canal. Ships from Asia enter through the Gulf of Aden and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, then travel north through the Red Sea towards the Suez Canal. This route significantly reduces travel distance and time between Asia and Europe compared to the alternative route around the Cape of Good Hope. Major ports and nearby maritime regions make it an important centre for global trade and energy transportation. The strategic importance of the Red Sea is highlighted by its narrow chokepoints, where disruptions can cause shipping delays, higher freight costs and supply-chain challenges.

    International shipping traffic connects major production centres, ports and markets across the world through oceans and strategically important maritime routes. Major routes link Asia–Europe, Asia–North America, the Persian Gulf–Asia and Asia–Africa–Europe. Ships navigate through critical chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz, Strait of Malacca, Suez Canal, Bab-el-Mandeb and Panama Canal. These routes carry containerised goods, crude oil, LNG, bulk commodities and other essential cargo. Any disruption at a major chokepoint can cause rerouting, longer voyages, higher freight and insurance costs, and global supply-chain impacts.

    The Black Sea is a major maritime trade region connecting Eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia with global markets. Ships access the Mediterranean through the Turkish Straits, passing through the Bosporus, Sea of Marmara and Dardanelles. Major ports such as Odesa, Constanța, Novorossiysk and Batumi support the movement of grain, oil, metals and other cargo. The Danube River also connects the Black Sea with important inland markets in Europe. Its strategic location makes it significant for international trade, energy security and regional geopolitics.

currentAffairs.Title: Battle of Haifa (1918): Indian Valour, Imperial Legacy and the Politics of Historical Memory
currentAffairs.Category:
GS Paper I – Modern Indian History, World History
GS Paper II – International Relations
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: The Battle of Haifa (1918) highlights the courage and contribution of Indian soldiers during the First World War and its lasting place in India’s military history. It also explores the contrasting memories of India, Israel and Palestine, revealing the complex legacy of colonial warfare, liberation and historical remembrance.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Battle of Haifa (1918): Indian Valour, Imperial Legacy and the Politics of Historical Memory

SYLLABUS AREAS:

GS Paper I – Modern Indian History, World History

GS Paper II – International Relations

1. The September 23, 1918 Battle of Haifa occupies a curious place in the intertwined histories of India, Israel, and Palestine. What was, in military terms, a small but tactically significant cavalry action in the final phase of the First World War has, over the past century, become a site of layered remembrance, celebrated, contested, reclaimed, and reinterpreted by different communities for different purposes.

2. For India, Haifa is often invoked as a symbol of the extraordinary global footprint of Indian soldiers during the First World War. More than a million Indians served overseas, from Flanders to Mesopotamia, and over 74,000 died in a war not of their own making. The cavalry charge at Haifa, executed by the Jodhpur, Mysore, and Hyderabad Lancers, stands out as one of the most dramatic episodes of Indian valour abroad.

3. For India, celebrating the battle (and renaming a First World War memorial as "Teen Murti Haifa Chowk") is a way of acknowledging that its soldiers shaped world events long before the country became a sovereign republic. For Israel, the memory of Indian cavalry "liberating" Haifa has been woven into a narrative of gratitude and friendship, symbolised by memorials and annual ceremonies. These commemorations serve diplomatic purposes, but they also reflect a genuine historical connection.

4. In the decades since Independence, Haifa has become part of a broader effort to reclaim India’s military history from the shadow of the empire. The soldiers who fought there were colonial subjects, but their courage and sacrifice belong to India’s national story. Commemorating Haifa thus becomes an act of historical recovery: an assertion that Indian agency existed even within the constraints of imperial command.

5. The Indian cavalry’s victory helped secure British control over Palestine, enabling the implementation of the Balfour Declaration and the subsequent political transformations that led to the creation of Israel. For many Palestinians, this is not a story of liberation but of dispossession. When Palestinian representatives say to Indians celebrating the Battle of Haifa, “We did not ask you to liberate us,” they are not questioning the bravery of Indian soldiers but the imperial project in which that bravery was embedded.

6. The Palestinian critique of the Haifa narrative adds another layer of complexity. For Palestinians, the 1918 campaign is part of a longer story of foreign domination and displacement. From their perspective, the Indian cavalry’s victory facilitated British rule and the subsequent transformations that reshaped their homeland. This view does not diminish the bravery of Indian soldiers, but it challenges celebratory narratives that ignore the lived experience of those who were "liberated".

currentAffairs.Short_Summary: India’s urban waste-management efforts are shifting from conventional dumping towards scientific legacy dumpsite remediation, resource recovery and sustainable land use under SBM-U 2.0. Case studies from Gorakhpur, Bhalswa, Nagpur and Raichur highlight how reclaimed dumpsites can become eco-parks, processing facilities and ecological spaces.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Urban Waste Management and Legacy Dumpsite Remediation

Syllabus areas:

GS Paper I – Indian Society

GS Paper II – Governance

GS Paper III – Environment & Ecology, Infrastructure, Economy

Urban cleanliness depends on an extensive waste-management system handling waste from households, markets, institutions, commercial establishments and public spaces. Over time, accumulated waste at dumpsites creates legacy waste sites. To address urban sanitation challenges, the Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban (SBM-U) was launched in October 2014, gradually expanding its focus from basic sanitation to scientific waste management.

Under SBM-U 2.0, launched in October 2021, cities are working to scientifically remediate legacy dumpsites and convert them into productive, environmentally sustainable spaces. Between January and December 2025, 3.66 crore metric tonnes of legacy waste were remediated, while 459 Urban Local Bodies across 29 States achieved complete dumpsite remediation. The Lakshya Zero Dumpsite initiative is driving this time-bound transformation across cities and States.

Case Study: Kachre Se Kanchan Rapti Eco Park, Gorakhpur

A 40-acre dumpsite in Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh, accumulated municipal waste for seven years. Through scientific biomining, waste was processed into fuel, black soil and inert material. The reclaimed site was transformed into Kachre Se Kanchan Rapti Eco Park, featuring green spaces, recreation facilities, solar lighting and water conservation structures, while supporting livelihoods through Shakti Ki Rasoi.

Case Study: Bhalswa Dumpsite, Delhi

The 70-acre Bhalswa dumpsite has undergone continuous biomining since July 2022. Under the Dumpsite Remediation Accelerator Programme (DRAP), launched in 2025, remediation was accelerated. By July 2026, 99.07 lakh metric tonnes of legacy waste had been processed, with over half the site reclaimed, alongside fire prevention, leachate management and measures to prevent fresh waste accumulation.

Case Study: Bhandewadi, Nagpur

Nagpur transformed the Bhandewadi dumping yard from a legacy waste site into an Integrated Municipal Waste Processing Facility. Over 10 lakh metric tonnes of accumulated waste have been scientifically excavated and treated, reclaiming valuable land. The facility now enables material recovery, composting and waste-derived fuel production, supported by dust control, leachate treatment and real-time monitoring.

Case Study: Yakalaspura Dumpsite, Raichur

In Raichur, Karnataka, the 35-acre Yakalaspura dumpsite is being transformed through scientific legacy waste remediation. About 62,252 metric tonnes of waste have been processed, reclaiming nearly 22 acres. Around 5–7 acres now support a Miyawaki forest, with 60,000 bamboo and native saplings planted from June 2026, promoting biodiversity and sustainable urban development under “Toxic Waste to Ecological Wealth.”

The Movement beyond Clean up:

A reclaimed dumpsite is more than recovered land. It represents a changing approach to managing the waste generated by cities. Across Gorakhpur, Delhi, Nagpur and Raichur, the pattern is the same. Waste mountains are excavated, sorted and turned back into usable land.

Machines and plants alone cannot make this last. City Solid Waste Action Plans, progress on the SBM-U portal and annual Swachh Survekshan rankings keep the work on course long after the ribbon is cut. Infrastructure and institutions together turn a one-time clean up into a lasting system. Swachh Bharat Mission—Urban began with sanitation, but it has grown well beyond it. It is now reshaping how cities reclaim land, restore ecology and build public spaces where people live, work and gather.

currentAffairs.Title: Why Apple Faces CCPA Probe over User-Rights Issue
currentAffairs.Category:
GS Paper II – Governance
GS Paper III – Indian Economy
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: The CCPA’s probe into Apple examines whether software-related issues and warranty exclusions could unfairly shift repair costs onto consumers. The case highlights consumer rights, warranty obligations and regulation of unfair trade practices.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Why Apple Faces CCPA Probe over User-Rights Issue

Syllabus Areas:

GS Paper II – Governance

GS Paper III – Indian Economy

The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) is investigating Apple’s software warranty terms following complaints about problems allegedly experienced by users after the rollout of iOS 18.

The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) is India’s consumer protection regulator, established under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, to safeguard consumer rights and address unfair trade practices.

Apple’s software warranty terms generally exclude software-related damage, including issues caused by iOS updates, while hardware defects may remain covered under standard warranty provisions.

The issue concerns whether consumers should bear repair costs when a software update is alleged to have triggered hardware-related problems, and whether Apple’s warranty terms and repair practices could amount to an unfair trade practice.

What is the CCPA Investigating?

Apple began rolling out iOS 18 in 2024. Following the rollout, some users reported various problems, including:

· Green, pink or white lines appearing on displays

· Microphone and call failures

· Frozen screens

· Battery drain

· Touchscreen malfunctions

· Camera malfunctions

Some users also reported that they were asked to pay for repairs. Replacing an iPhone 15 screen costs about ₹27,900.

The CCPA is examining whether consumers should bear such costs when the alleged trigger was Apple’s software. It is also examining whether the company’s warranty terms and repair practices amount to an unfair trade practice.

The CCPA first issued Apple a notice in 2025 and has subsequently escalated the matter to its investigation wing.

Apple’s Position

Apple is contesting the regulator’s allegations. The company has stated that the case was based on 70 complaints and has denied that iOS 18 has a systemic problem in India.

In its response dated 20 August, Apple stated that the software had undergone stringent testing. It also noted that only around 11% of iPhones were still running iOS 18 as of June 2026.

Apple has defended its software warranty terms, pointing out that its licence agreements state that the software is provided without any warranty.

The company has also stated that it would work with the regulator to provide clarity regarding how it responded to customers who reported problems with their iPhones.

What is the Warranty Issue?

Apple’s standard warranty covers defects in materials and workmanship in the device’s hardware, but generally does not cover damage caused by iOS, including updates.

This creates a grey area when a software patch is alleged to have triggered a hardware problem.

In such cases, users may have to pay for repairs if Apple determines that the fault falls outside the scope of warranty coverage.

Can Consumer Law Override Warranty Terms?

A warranty is a contractual arrangement between a firm and a consumer. However, its terms do not automatically insulate a firm from its obligations under India’s consumer protection laws.

The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 empowers authorities to examine practices that may amount to unfair trade practices or may mislead consumers and to direct corrective action.

Although a warranty may specify the types of defects or repairs that Apple will cover, the CCPA can examine whether consumers were unfairly made to bear repair costs.

Implications for Other Companies

Apple is not the only company that distinguishes between hardware warranties and software.

Google’s India warranty explicitly covers hardware and excludes software elements.

OnePlus states that its limited warranty does not cover, or only partially covers, software and excludes certain software-related problems.

Samsung’s terms also state that it does not take responsibility for the quality of software.

Similarly, Xiaomi, Vivo and Realme frame their warranties with various exclusions.

Therefore, the CCPA’s conclusion in the matter could have implications for other phone manufacturers as well.

currentAffairs.Title: Chronic Kidney Disease of Unknown Origin: Uddanam Nephropathy
currentAffairs.Category:
GS Paper II – Social Justice | 
GS Paper III – Environment & Ecology, Science & Technology | 
Essay
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: This article examines Uddanam Nephropathy (CKDu), a chronic kidney disease of unknown origin affecting agricultural communities in Andhra Pradesh. It explores the possible links with heat stress, dehydration, environmental exposure and other factors, along with similar kidney diseases reported globally.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Chronic Kidney Disease of Unknown Origin: Uddanam Nephropathy

Syllabus areas:

GS Paper II – Social Justice

GS Paper III – Environment & Ecology, Science & Technology

Essay

1. What is Uddanam Nephropathy?

Uddanam Nephropathy, also referred to as Chronic Kidney Disease of Unknown Origin (CKDu), is a kidney disease reported in the Uddanam region of Andhra Pradesh.

The disease was first reported in the 1990s and has affected tens of thousands of people in the region, primarily agricultural workers, leading to significant morbidity and mortality.

The exact cause of the disease remains unknown. Patients did not have swollen feet or hands and did not have a history of elevated protein levels in urine.

2. Uddanam and CKDu

Uddanam is a region in the Srikakulam district of Andhra Pradesh, covering the mandals of:

· Ichchapuram

· Kanchili

· Kaviti

· Sompeta

· Vajrapu Kothuru

· Mandasa

· Palasa

The population of the region was over 5,50,000 in the 2011 Census and 8,00,000 by 2021.

Uddanam has drawn national and international attention due to the high prevalence of mysterious chronic kidney disease known as Uddanam Nephropathy/CKDu.

3. Similar Kidney Diseases Across Different Regions

There are similar forms of kidney disease reported in other agricultural regions of the world.

Balkan Endemic Nephropathy

A similar condition has been reported in the farming villages of Europe's Balkan Peninsula.

Scientists found birthwort, a plant with a weedy stem growing thick in wheat fields. Compounds called aristolochic acids were identified as the cause of severe kidney disease, besides cancer.

This condition is called Balkan Endemic Nephropathy.

Mesoamerican Nephropathy

Another such condition is called Mesoamerican Nephropathy.

It is:

· Non-diabetic and non-hypertensive chronic kidney disease

· Prevalent in agricultural communities along the Pacific Ocean coastal lowlands

· Reported in Mesoamerica, including:

o Mexico

o Guatemala

o El Salvador

o Nicaragua

o Honduras

o Costa Rica

Sri Lanka and Other Indian Regions

Similar nephropathy has also been reported in Sri Lanka.

Coastal agricultural pockets of Odisha, Goa and Maharashtra have also reported conditions similar to Uddanam.

In Tamil Nadu, 8% of the population has kidney disease, and among them, half has no identifiable cause.

4. Possible Causes

The causes associated with such kidney diseases include:

Extreme Heat and Dehydration

Extreme heat and resulting dehydration are considered possible factors. The focus is on drinking 2 litres of water a day.

Excessive Salt Intake

Too much salt intake, mostly from ultra-processed food, can lead to excess sodium. Excess sodium can damage the lining of blood vessels, even in people who do not have blood pressure problems.

Groundwater

Groundwater used as drinking water in India has a risk of high salt and metal content, likely caused by pesticides or industrial pollution.

The kidneys are particularly vulnerable as they are the primary organs responsible for filtering these toxins from the blood.

5. CKDu and Other Common Kidney Problems

CKDu

In CKDu:

· The cause is unknown.

· Patients generally do not have diabetes or hypertension.

· The disease is particularly associated with young and middle-aged agricultural workers in hot rural areas.

· Suspected links include heat stress, dehydration, agrochemicals and heavy metals.

· Prevention remains unclear, with focus on hydration, reducing agrochemical exposure and avoiding heat stress.

· It is mainly associated with farming regions.

Other Common Kidney Problems

Other common kidney problems usually have a known cause.

CKD – Chronic Kidney Disease can be associated with:

· Diabetes

· Hypertension

· Glomerulonephritis

· Polycystic kidney disease

AKI – Acute Kidney Injury can be associated with:

· Infections

· Toxins

· Dehydration

· Obstruction

· Sepsis

CKD is more common among the elderly, diabetics and hypertensives, while kidney disease can affect anyone and occurs globally.

Measures mentioned include controlling diabetes and hypertension, treating infections and avoiding nephrotoxic drugs.

6. Nephrotoxic Drugs

Some drugs and substances can be harmful to the kidneys, including:

1. Antibiotics

2. Antivirals

3. Pain killers – reduce blood flow to the kidneys by blocking prostaglandins

4. Chemotherapy drugs

5. Immunosuppressants

6. Radiologic contrast agents – used in CT scans and angiography

7. Lithium – used in bipolar disorder

8. Proton pump inhibitors – long-term use of Omeprazole, Pantoprazole and Rabeprazole

9. Certain herbal medicines containing aristolochic acid

Conclusion

Uddanam Nephropathy/CKDu represents a form of chronic kidney disease in which the usual causes such as diabetes and hypertension do not explain the condition. Its occurrence among agricultural communities, along with similar kidney diseases reported in other farming regions, has drawn national and international attention. The exact cause remains unclear, with heat stress, dehydration, agrochemicals, heavy metals and other environmental factors among the suspected links.

MCQ’s

Q1. A village reports increasing kidney disease among agricultural workers but has relatively low prevalence of conventional metabolic risk factors. Which investigation would be most relevant initially for understanding the cluster?

A. Only screening for diabetes

B. Only measuring blood pressure

C. Assessing occupational heat exposure, hydration, agrochemical use and environmental contaminants along with clinical data

D. Assuming a hereditary disorder because conventional causes are absent

Answer: C

Q2. A disease cluster occurring predominantly among agricultural workers in hot regions necessarily proves that heat exposure is its cause.

A. True B. False

Answer: B

Q3. Consider the following statements regarding nephrotoxic exposures:

  • Some analgesics can affect renal blood flow through inhibition of prostaglandin-mediated mechanisms.
  • Certain chemotherapeutic agents can have nephrotoxic effects.
  • Radiological contrast agents are completely irrelevant to renal function.
  • Aristolochic acid exposure has been associated with serious renal disease.

    • Which of the statements given above are correct?

    A. 1 and 2 only B. 1, 2 and 4 only C. 2, 3 and 4 only D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

    Answer: B

    Q4. Which of the following combinations best represents a One Health/environmental-health perspective on CKDu?

    A. Kidney disease → hospital treatment → pharmaceutical intervention

    B. Agricultural work → heat exposure → water stress → environmental contaminants → renal risk

    C. Diabetes → obesity → hypertension → CKD

    D. Infection → antibiotics → immunity → kidney recovery

    Answer: B

    Q5.

    Assertion (A): Occupational heat exposure can be relevant to the study of unexplained kidney disease among agricultural workers.

    Reason (R): Repeated dehydration can impose physiological stress on the kidneys, particularly where workers have prolonged exposure to heat.

    A. Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A B. Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A C. A is true, but R is false D. A is false, but R is true

    Answer: A

The article examines its evolution, organizational structure, operational role and contribution to India’s internal security framework.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Grey Hounds

Syllabus Areas:

Essay

GS Paper I – Indian Society

GS Paper II – Governance

GS Paper III – Internal Security

The Grey Hounds was born out of a realisation that conventional policing was proving inadequate against the growing influence and armed strength of Maoists. The then Andhra Pradesh Government wanted a force that could take the fight into forests and match the insurgents on their own terrain.

In 1989, IPS officer K.S. Vyas created Greyhounds to combat the Maoist insurgency. Within a few years, the striking force had evolved into one of the country’s most specialised counter-insurgency units, operating deep inside forests and developing tactics specifically suited to jungle warfare. It also became a model for other states seeking to create specialised units to fight insurgency in different terrain.

  • Odisha – Special Operation Group
  • Maharashtra – C-60
  • West Bengal – Counter-Insurgency Force
  • Chhattisgarh – District Reserve Guard

    • Even the CRPF’s elite Commando Battalion for Resolute Action (COBRA) drew from the Greyhounds model.

    When DIG Vyas took charge on June 15, 1989, the Greyhounds was a 350-member force, with nearly 90% of its personnel being constables. Vyas headed the unit until March 30, 1990. Over the years, its strength grew to over 2,000 at its peak. Today, following Union Home Minister Amit Shah’s declaration in May that the country was Naxal-free, the force has 650 personnel, an officer says.

    In the erstwhile Andhra Pradesh, the Greyhounds had 41 units, each comprising 35 personnel including a DSP, an inspector and three sub-inspectors. There is no separate recruitment for the force. It is a deputation-based unit, with personnel volunteering from the Special Police, Armed Reserve and Civil Police.

    Those seeking a posting with the Greyhounds are screened for physical fitness, mental resilience and the determination required for the job. Personnel deputed to the force receive 60% of their basic pay and dearness allowance for the duration of their posting.

    Cost of the war

    The Greyhounds carried out numerous operations over the years, neutralising hundreds of rebels across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. There were also instances when its teams crossed into neighbouring Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh to strike targets operating from across State borders.

    But the striking force had another backbone: intelligence. At the heart of the Greyhounds’ success was the Special Intelligence Branch (SIB), another specialised unit that emerged alongside the force to track the movement and activities of the rebels.

    Since its inception, the Greyhounds has neutralised 693 rebels in undivided Andhra Pradesh and seized 1,250 firearms, Kumar says. Following the formation of Telangana on June 2, 2014, the force has killed 92 Naxals and recovered 360 weapons, he adds.

    But the fight against the Red Army came at a heavy cost. The Greyhounds lost over 60 men over the years, including six after the formation of Telangana.

    One of its biggest setbacks came on June 29, 2008, when Maoists ambushed a team on the Balimela reservoir in Odisha, killing 37 people, including 32 commandos.

    The Greyhounds team had crossed into Odisha in pursuit of Maoists who had taken shelter there. Unable to locate them, the commandos were returning when Maoists, who had laid an ambush around the reservoir, opened fire on their boat.

    The attack sank the boat and became one of the darkest chapters in the force’s history.

currentAffairs.Title: India’s Path to Blue Skies: From Awareness to Action for Cleaner Air
currentAffairs.Category: GS III - Environment
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: India’s clean-air strategy combines monitoring, NCAP, digital tracking, sector-wise pollution control, green initiatives, and coordinated governance to achieve cleaner air and healthier communities.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Syllabus Areas:

GS III - Environment

Clean air is fundamental to human health, environmental sustainability and economic well-being. With rapid urbanisation and economic activity, air pollution has emerged as an important global environmental challenge.

The International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies, observed annually on 7 September, highlights the need for stronger action against air pollution. The 2026 campaign focuses on increasing public awareness, facilitating action against air pollution and aligning global efforts with national priorities.

India has adopted a multi-sectoral and science-based approach involving air-quality monitoring, emission control, city-specific action plans, policy interventions and institutional strengthening.

Controlling particulate pollution is therefore an important component of efforts towards cleaner air and healthier communities.

Real-Time Air Quality Monitoring

India uses multiple monitoring systems to track ambient air quality and pollution from industrial sources.

Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring System (CAAQMS)

CAAQMS enables real-time monitoring of air quality and tracks pollutants including:

  • PM10
  • PM2.5
  • Sulphur Dioxide (SO₂)
  • Nitrogen Oxides (NOx)
  • Carbon Monoxide (CO)
  • Ozone (O₃)

    • It also monitors meteorological parameters such as:

  • Wind direction
  • Wind speed
  • Temperature
  • Humidity

    • Ambient Air Quality Monitoring System (AAQMS)

  • AAQMS is a broader framework involving both manual and automated monitoring of air pollutants.
  • Manual monitoring involves collection of samples over specified periods, while automated systems provide continuous measurements.

    • Online Continuous Emission Monitoring System (OCEMS)

    OCEMS monitors emissions directly from industrial sources.

  • It is particularly relevant for highly polluting industries and enables industries and regulators to monitor emissions continuously and transmit data to the CPCB.
  • This strengthens regulatory compliance and supports enforcement against industries exceeding prescribed standards

    • Sector-Wise Measures to Improve Air Quality

  • Vehicular Emissions: BS-VI norms, EV promotion, vehicle scrappage and expansion of electric/public transport.
  • Industrial Emissions: Stricter emission standards, particulate-matter norms and OCEMS for continuous monitoring.
  • Road Dust: Water sprinkling, mechanised road sweeping, covering construction materials and anti-smog measures.
  • Construction Activities: Dust-control measures and compliance monitoring at construction sites.
  • C&D Waste: Scientific collection, recycling, disposal and implementation of C&D Waste Management Rules.
  • Open Waste Burning: Stronger enforcement of waste-management rules and Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR).
  • Crop-Residue Burning: Biomass pelletisation, co-firing in power plants, residue-management machinery and alternative uses.
  • Green Cover: Green India Mission, CAMPA, Nagar Van Yojana and Aravalli Green Wall Initiative.
  • Institutions: CPCB, CAQM and SPCBs undertake monitoring, regulation, coordination and enforcement.
  • GRAP: AQI-based graded action plan in NCR to control pollution through restrictions on construction, vehicles, industries and dust.

    • India's approach to cleaner air is increasingly moving from awareness to measurement, monitoring, targeted intervention and institutional coordination. The combination of city-specific action plans, real-time monitoring, industrial regulation, cleaner mobility, dust and waste management, crop-residue management and ecological restoration represents a multi-dimensional strategy.

    The long-term challenge is to translate these programmes into sustained improvements in ambient air quality, supported by scientific evidence, effective enforcement, local implementation and citizen participation.

currentAffairs.Category:
