currentAffairs.Short_Summary:
The reintroduction of the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions has raised questions about its impact on digital payment usage.
This article examines the scope of MDR, its implications for merchants and users, and its role in strengthening the UPI ecosystem and digital payments infrastructure.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
UPI Merchant Discount Rate (MDR): Will It Affect UPI Usage?

Syllabus Areas:

GS Paper I – Society

GS Paper II – Governance

GS Paper III – Economy

The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has reintroduced the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on certain Person-to-Merchant (P2M) UPI transactions. The move has raised concerns about whether charging merchants could affect the volume and widespread use of UPI payments.

However, the majority of UPI transactions will continue to remain free, and the impact on overall transaction volumes is expected to be limited.

What is Merchant Discount Rate (MDR)?

Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) is a fee associated with digital payments made to merchants. Under the revised arrangement, the charge is applicable only to certain eligible P2M UPI transactions.

The fee is charged to merchants and not consumers. NPCI has also prohibited payment application providers from imposing additional platform fees on users.

Will MDR Affect UPI Transaction Volumes?

The reintroduction of MDR is not expected to significantly affect overall UPI transaction volumes because only around 4% of total UPI transactions are expected to be eligible for the charge, according to the Finance Ministry.

The following transactions will continue to remain free:

  • All Person-to-Person (P2P) UPI transactions
  • P2M UPI transactions of up to ₹2,000

    • Since most transactions will not attract MDR, transaction volumes are expected to remain largely steady. However, some minor declines may occur in high-value and active commercial transactions, particularly as banks and payment service providers adjust their back-end processes.

    The key issue will be how merchants and different sectors absorb the additional charges.

    Which Other Payments Will Remain Free or Receive Relief?

    Within P2M transactions, small merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh per month through UPI QR codes will not be charged MDR.

    Similarly, auto-debit recurring payments, known as UPI mandates or UPI AutoPay, will not carry MDR charges.

    For transactions above ₹2,000 in certain essential and thin-margin sectors, including:

  • Railways
  • Telecommunications
  • Insurance
  • Fuel
  • Utility-bill payments
  • Educational fees
  • Agricultural inputs

    • a flat MDR of ₹5 per transaction will apply.

    Payments related to mutual funds, securities, stockbrokers and dealers will attract an MDR of 0.02%, subject to a maximum cap of ₹300.

    How Can MDR Support the UPI Ecosystem?

    The MDR collected will be distributed among different players in the UPI ecosystem and can contribute towards the growth and security of UPI.

    The government recommends allocating 5% of the collections towards infrastructure for smaller merchants.

    These measures are expected to help:

  • Enable expansion into new markets
  • Enhance load capacity
  • Strengthen infrastructure
  • Tighten fraud prevention
  • Drive innovation

    • Thus, MDR can provide resources for maintaining and upgrading the infrastructure supporting the UPI ecosystem.

    Could Merchants and Users Shift Away from UPI?

    With the majority of UPI transactions continuing to face zero MDR, transaction volumes are likely to remain largely steady.

    Some minor decline could occur in high-value commercial transactions, particularly while banks and payment service providers calibrate their systems. However, industry experts expect long-term growth to remain on track.

    There is also a possibility that some merchants could return to cash payments. Users could potentially shift towards other payment methods, such as digital wallets or the Central Bank Digital Currency (e-rupee), which continue to be free.

    Will Consumers Have to Pay More?

    At present, MDR is charged to merchants rather than consumers. Therefore, users are not directly required to pay the MDR.

    Merchants generally absorb such operational costs because of the benefits associated with higher sales volumes and reduced cash-handling risks.

    However, in the case of large transactions, merchants have historically passed on payment-related costs to customers through surcharges or convenience fees, as is seen with credit cards.

    Whether merchants will adopt similar methods to recover MDR costs for large UPI transactions remains to be seen.

    UPI and the E-Rupee

    The reintroduction of MDR also comes at a time when the Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC), or e-rupee, can be further popularised as an alternative digital payment mechanism.

    While UPI provides a convenient payment mechanism, it operates through banks. In contrast, e-rupee wallets operated by the central bank could enable digital currency to function more like cash, without intermediary risk.

    The e-rupee has the same financial status as an “IOU” issued directly by the monetary authority.

    The underlying technology of digital currencies also has the potential to shape the future of money globally. Therefore, keeping pace with developments in digital currencies remains important.

    Conclusion

    The reintroduction of MDR represents a selective shift in the UPI payment ecosystem rather than a charge applicable to all UPI transactions. With P2P payments and P2M transactions up to ₹2,000 remaining free, the majority of users are not directly affected.

    At the same time, MDR can provide financial resources for UPI infrastructure, cybersecurity, fraud prevention and innovation. The extent to which merchants absorb these costs or pass them on through other charges will determine its broader effect on the UPI ecosystem.

currentAffairs.Title: How India Became a Major Destination for Wild Animals
currentAffairs.Category: GS Paper III – Environment & Ecology
currentAffairs.Short_Summary:
Explore why India has emerged as a major destination for international wildlife imports, particularly for zoos and captive conservation facilities.
Understand the UPSC relevance through **CITES, wildlife trade, ex-situ conservation, animal welfare, and India’s regulatory framework**.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
How India Became a Major Destination for Wild Animals

Syllabus relevance:

GS Paper III – Environment & Ecology

A report titled “How India became No.1 destination for wild animals” highlighted the growing movement of wild animals from different countries into India, particularly for zoos and captive facilities. The report points to a sharp rise in the number and diversity of animals entering Indian zoological institutions in recent years. Importantly, the phrase “No.1 destination” refers to international movement/import of animals for zoos and related purposes, and not to natural migration of wild animals into India.

1. Why are wild animals brought to India?

International movement of animals may take place for several legitimate purposes:

  • Conservation breeding programmes
  • Exchange between zoological institutions
  • Scientific research and education
  • Genetic management of captive populations
  • Rescue and rehabilitation
  • Development of recognised zoological facilities
  • Species restoration and reintroduction programmes

    • However, importing animals also requires adequate veterinary facilities, quarantine arrangements, suitable habitats, trained personnel and long-term financial resources.

    2. CITES – The Key International Framework

    The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) regulates international trade in wild animals and plants so that such trade does not threaten their survival.

    CITES classifies species into three Appendices:

    Appendix I: Species threatened with extinction; international commercial trade is generally prohibited.

    Appendix II: Species that may become threatened unless trade is regulated; controlled international trade is permitted.

    Appendix III: Species protected in at least one country that seeks cooperation from other countries to control trade.

    India is a Party to CITES, and its international wildlife-trade framework operates through domestic legislation and regulatory authorities.

    3. India's Legal and Institutional Framework

    The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 is the principal legislation for wildlife protection in India. International wildlife trade is also linked with the Customs Act, 1962 and the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992.

    Important institutions include:

  • Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) – overall policy framework
  • Central Zoo Authority (CZA) – regulation and standards relating to zoos
  • Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB) – prevention and enforcement against wildlife crime
  • Directorate of Wildlife Preservation – important role in implementation of CITES-related controls
  • Customs authorities – regulation and detection of illegal wildlife movement at international borders

    • The CZA also deals with zoo animal exchanges, subject to the required clearances and CITES permits.

    4. Ex-situ vs In-situ Conservation

    In-situ conservation means conserving species in their natural habitats, such as national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves.

    Ex-situ conservation involves conservation outside the natural habitat, including:

  • Zoos
  • Captive-breeding centres
  • Gene banks
  • Botanical gardens

    • Zoos can contribute to conservation breeding, public awareness and scientific research. However, captive conservation cannot completely replace protection of species in their natural ecosystems.

    5. Conservation vs. Wildlife Trade

    The increasing movement of animals across borders raises an important governance question: When does movement of wildlife serve conservation, and when can it become commercial exploitation or contribute to illegal trade?

    Key concerns include:

  • Animal welfare and quality of captivity
  • Disease transmission and quarantine
  • Genetic diversity of captive populations
  • Availability of suitable enclosures and veterinary care
  • Transparency in international animal transfers
  • Risk of illegal wildlife trafficking
  • Whether imports produce measurable conservation benefits

    • CITES itself distinguishes between regulated legal trade and illegal wildlife trafficking. India has also strengthened enforcement against wildlife crime through agencies such as the WCCB.

    6. Do Not Confuse Zoo Imports with Project Cheetah

    zoo imports and conservation translocation.

    Under Project Cheetah, eight cheetahs were brought from Namibia and released in Kuno National Park on 17 September 2022. Twelve more were subsequently translocated from South Africa in February 2023. The project aims at restoring a species that had become extinct in India and rebuilding a free-ranging population.

    Therefore:

    Zoo import → captive management/ex-situ purposes

    Conservation translocation → restoration or establishment of wild populations

    Wildlife trafficking → illegal movement or trade

    India's growing role in the international movement of wild animals highlights the intersection of biodiversity conservation, international wildlife trade, CITES, animal welfare and environmental governance. For UPSC preparation, the focus should therefore be on the regulatory framework, conservation objectives and challenges associated with transboundary wildlife movement, rather than simply memorising import numbers.

A quick-reference guide to essential helplines that every citizen should know and save for times of need.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Important Helpline Numbers in India and the World

Syllabus areas:

  • GS Paper I – Indian Society: Vulnerable Sections of Society
  • GS Paper III – Internal Security: Cyber Security
  • GS Paper III – Science & Technology: Information Technology
  • GS Paper IV – Ethics: Probity in Governance

    • Helplines are dedicated telephone services that provide citizens with emergency assistance, information, grievance redressal, counselling, protection and access to government services. Their administration may be national, state-specific, or jointly implemented by Central and State authorities.

    1098 – CHILDLINE – first launched helpline in India

  • Started: 1996
  • Area: Child protection and assistance
  • Origin: Began as a field-action project of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS), Mumbai
  • Purpose: Assistance to children in distress, including abandoned, abused, homeless and vulnerable children.
  • It later developed into a nationwide child helpline under the Government of India.

    • 1. Major National Helplines in India

    1. Emergency Numbers

    112 – Unified Emergency Helpline Single emergency number for police, fire, ambulance and other emergency assistance across India.

    1033 – NHAI Highway Helpline For emergencies and assistance on National Highways, including accidents, vehicle breakdowns and highway-related issues.

    1070 – Disaster Management Helpline A toll-free number for State/Central Relief Commissioners and State Emergency Operation Centres to coordinate and respond to natural disasters and emergencies.

    2. Women Helpline

    181 – Women Helpline Provides assistance, counselling and support to women facing violence, harassment, abuse or other distress situations.

    3. Child Helpline

    1098 – Child Helpline A dedicated helpline for children in distress, including cases of abuse, abandonment, trafficking, exploitation and other emergencies.

    4. Senior Citizens / Persons with Disabilities

    14567 – Elderline National helpline for senior citizens providing information, guidance, emotional support and assistance regarding welfare and grievances.

    14456 – National Disability Helpline Provides information and assistance to Persons with Disabilities regarding government schemes, disability services, rights and support mechanisms.

    5. Enquiry / Citizen Services

    139 – Indian Railways Helpline Provides railway-related information and assistance, including train services, passenger grievances and railway enquiries.

    1947 – Aadhaar Helpline UIDAI helpline for Aadhaar-related information, enrolment, updates, authentication and other Aadhaar services.

    1950 – Voter Helpline Election Commission helpline for voter registration, electoral-roll information, EPIC-related services and election-related queries.

    6. Other Important Helplines

    1930 – National Cyber Crime Helpline For reporting cyber financial fraud and seeking immediate assistance to prevent further loss of money.

    14416 – Tele-MANAS 24×7 national tele-mental-health helpline providing counselling, psychological support and referral services.

    1906 – LPG Emergency Helpline Dedicated emergency helpline for reporting LPG leakage and seeking immediate assistance.

    Major Helplines Introduced During the Modi Government Period

    The Government of India has introduced and strengthened several citizen-centric helplines in recent years to improve emergency response, cybercrime prevention, mental healthcare and welfare delivery.

    1. 1930 – National Cyber Crime Helpline

    · Ministry: Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)

    · Nodal Institution: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C)

    · Introduced: CFCFRMS was launched in 2021; the 1930 helpline was subsequently operationalised for assistance in reporting cyber financial fraud.

    · Purpose: Enables citizens to report financial cyber fraud quickly and facilitates coordination with banks and law-enforcement agencies to prevent further loss of funds.

    2. 14567 – Elderline

    · Ministry: Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment

    · Launched: 2021

    · Purpose: India’s first Pan-India toll-free helpline dedicated to senior citizens. It provides information, legal and pension-related guidance, emotional support and intervention in cases of elder abuse or abandonment.

    · UPSC Linkage: Ageing population, social justice, welfare of vulnerable sections and inclusive governance.

    3. 14416 – Tele-MANAS

    · Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

    · Launched: 10 October 2022

    · Purpose: Provides 24×7 tele-mental health services across India, including counselling, psychological support and referral services.

    · Other Number: 1-800-891-4416

    · UPSC Linkage: Mental health, public health, digital healthcare and accessibility of healthcare services.

    4. 112 – Emergency Response Support System (ERSS)

    · Ministry: Ministry of Home Affairs

    · National Rollout: 2018–19

    · Purpose: A unified emergency number integrating police, fire, health and other emergency services. It replaced the need to remember multiple emergency numbers in participating areas.

    · UPSC Linkage: Police reforms, emergency management, technology-enabled governance and citizen-centric administration.

    5. 1075 – National COVID-19 Health Helpline

    · Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

    · Introduced: 2020

    · Purpose: Provided citizens with information and guidance related to COVID-19, including symptoms, testing, treatment and government advisories.

    · UPSC Linkage: Pandemic management, public health, disaster management and crisis communication.

    2. Important Scam/Fraud-Related Helpline

    1930 – Cyber Financial Fraud

    This is particularly important in the context of the growing digital economy and online scams.

    Citizens can report financial cyber fraud through 1930 and the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. The CFCFRMS enables rapid reporting and coordination with banks, financial intermediaries and State/UT law-enforcement agencies to help prevent further loss.

    3. National vs State Helplines

    Not every helpline number in India is centrally controlled.

    National helplines: Generally operate across India and are established by Central institutions/agencies.

    State helplines: Operated by State Governments for state-specific services such as electricity, public grievances, transport and local administration.

    Implementation can also be shared. For example, cybercrime is a State subject for investigation and prosecution, while the Central Government provides national mechanisms such as I4C, NCRP and CFCFRMS.

    Therefore, UPSC aspirants should distinguish between “national number” and “centrally administered service.”

    4. Unique International Helpline System

    A particularly interesting international example is the European Union's 116 numbering range.

    The 116 series is reserved for harmonised social-value services:

  • 116 000 – Missing Children
  • 116 111 – Child Helpline
  • 116 123 – Emotional Support
  • 116 006 – Victims of Crime
  • 116 016 – Violence against Women
  • 116 117 – Non-emergency Medical Assistance

    • This is significant because several European countries use harmonised numbers for similar social services, facilitating easier access across borders.

    Other internationally recognised emergency numbers include:

  • 911 – USA: Police, fire and medical emergencies
  • 999 – UK: Police, fire and ambulance
  • 000 – Australia: Emergency services
  • 111 – New Zealand: Emergency services
  • 112 – European Union: Emergency services

currentAffairs.Title: BRICS - Climate Change
currentAffairs.Category: GS II - International Relations | GS III - Environment and Ecology
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: BRICS as a platform for Global South cooperation on climate resilience, energy security, sustainable development, technology, climate finance, and green jobs
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Syllabus Areas:

GS II - International Relations | GS III - Environment and Ecology

Also Read Articles on BRICS and BRICS-India’s Vision

BRICS, representative of Global South, is a real counterpoint to G7. Today BRICS nations are not just third world economies. BRICS is an existential collaboration because to grow in a sustainable manner we are already seeing a potentially catastrophic impact of climate change, and the people most affected are in the Global South.
  • BRICS can achieve practical South-to-South problem solving around food security, sustainability, climate resilience, affordable and inclusive innovation and employing young people in a productive way.
  • BRICS is a historic opportunity and its potential is hosted by India because India is truly at the epicentre of all these complex dynamics.
  • Trumpian impacts made it clearer to BRICS how important energy independence and security are and much important renewable energy is.
  • For instance, India, always dependent on the oil-rich Gulf. China, which has a lot of oil reserves, today, China's auto industry and battery sector are world leaders.

    • Other BRICS economies are similarly visionary:

  • Consider Brazil, an astonishing country, a bit like India - very large, democratic and diverse. They understood the importance of energy security, sustainability and now Brazil is a new pioneer of biofuels. They have large amounts of forest cover and agricultural products. A lot of that bio-waste is used for making biofuels.
  • Russia has plenty of fossil fuels and it doesn't look like it may transition to renewable any time soon but China, India, Brazil and South Africa - rising economies - are on their path - The Trumpian era is making it clear to these nations that they have to be self-sufficient in energy.
  • India must meet its development needs and the challenge of raising a very large number of people out of poverty or lower middle income status. So there is a continuing fossil fuel dependence alongside other issues like transitioning the jobs of people working in mining etc.
  • Currently, India is not more sustainable than China or the west and we are still dependent on coal.
  • In terms of South-South problem-solving and working environmental resilience, there could be a BRICS Climate and Resilience Fund now, a real platform with significant funding.

    • The recent catastrophic floods in Nepal - submerging entire valleys, displacing hundreds of thousands and wiping out decades of development gains in 72 hours - are a case study in precisely what happens when world's most vulnerable communities are left waiting for a multilateral system that moves at the speed of diplomatic courtesy.

  • The green jobs opportunity is where the BRICS climate hub agreed - morally compelling but economically irresistible. India alone has the potential to generate 35 million green jobs by 2047.
  • Brazil's bioeconomy could employ 20 million in sustainable agriculture, forest restoration and green manufacturing by 2035.

currentAffairs.Full_Content:
BRICS: India's Vision

Syllabus areas

GS Paper II – International Relations

GS Paper III – Indian Economy

The BRICS Summit in New Delhi (September 12–13, 2026) takes place against the backdrop of geopolitical turbulence unleashed by a combination of forces: raging wars and conflicts, a breakdown in global governance, and the changing nature of global alliances.

It also takes place amid technological developments such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing, which are being weaponised, with both great powers trying to win the battle for technological supremacy.

BRICS has traditionally comprised three pillars:

1. Political and security

2. Finance and the economy

3. Culture and people-to-people exchanges

The theme is "Building Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability."

Resilience:

The work done by BRICS under India's stewardship has been stellar. This includes the launch of the BRICS Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage,

  • The adoption of the BRICS Logistics Supply Chain Cooperation Framework
  • The establishment of Centres of Excellence on Agro-Ecology and
  • Regenerative Agriculture.

    • Innovation:

    India has tried to push the envelope within BRICS. Proposals include a Start-up Innovation Fund,

  • An incubator network,
  • A Digital Public Infrastructure repository,
  • A Science and Research repository,

    • And an Action Plan of the BRICS Working Group on Research Infrastructures and Mega-Science Projects, which will be beneficial to all BRICS members.

    Cooperation:

  • Multilateral trading system
  • Network of Centres of Excellence on mental wellness
  • BRICS Urbanisation Forum
  • Digital capacity of women
  • And, broadly, intensifying cooperation in areas such as education, youth skilling, and the BRICS MSME (Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises) Cooperation Portal.

    • Sustainability:

  • Combating desertification
  • Developing guidelines for disaster management
  • Forest fire preparedness
  • Sustainable aviation fuels
  • Advancing climate resilience through people-centric
  • Community-based adaptation.

currentAffairs.Title: Sea Change: Five New Acts to Accelerate Growth in India’s Maritime Sector
currentAffairs.Category: GS Paper II: Government policies and interventions,GS Paper III: Infrastructure; ports and shipping
currentAffairs.Short_Summary:
India’s maritime sector is undergoing a major legal transformation through five new Acts aimed at modernising shipping, ports and coastal trade.

currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Sea Change: Five New Acts to Accelerate Growth in India’s Maritime Sector

Syllabus Areas

GS Paper II: Government policies and interventions; Centre-State relations; regulatory framework.

GS Paper III: Infrastructure; ports and shipping; logistics; Blue Economy; environmental sustainability; international trade.

Why in News?

India has undertaken a major overhaul of its maritime legal framework through five new legislations — the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025; Coastal Shipping Act, 2025; Indian Ports Act, 2025; Bills of Lading Act, 2025; and Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025.

The reforms seek to replace outdated legal provisions, simplify regulations, improve ease of doing business, strengthen maritime safety and align India’s maritime sector with international standards. The Bills of Lading Act and Carriage of Goods by Sea Act came into force from 10 September 2025.

India's maritime sector is crucial to its economy because a substantial share of the country's external trade by volume moves through the sea. Ports and shipping are therefore closely linked with trade, logistics, industrial development, energy security and employment.

The new laws seek to create a modern, integrated and globally aligned maritime governance framework, supporting India's broader objectives under Maritime Vision 2047.

What Are the Five New Acts?

1. Merchant Shipping Act, 2025

The Act modernises India's legal framework for merchant shipping and seeks to improve ease of doing business and regulatory clarity.

Key areas include:

  • Welfare and skill development of seafarers
  • Maritime safety and navigation
  • Protection of the marine environment
  • Alignment with International Maritime Organization (IMO) standards
  • Strengthening India's shipping capabilities

    • The reform is important for developing a competitive Indian merchant fleet and improving India's position in global maritime trade.

    2. Coastal Shipping Act, 2025

    The Act provides a dedicated framework for regulating and promoting coastal shipping.

    Coastal shipping can provide a cost-effective and relatively greener alternative to road-based freight transportation. The Act also seeks greater integration between coastal shipping and inland waterways.

    It simplifies the regulatory framework for Indian vessels engaged in coastal trade and provides for greater transparency through a public database.

    The larger objective is to increase the use of India's coastline for domestic freight movement while reducing logistics costs and congestion on land-based transport networks.

    3. Indian Ports Act, 2025

    The Act replaces the century-old Indian Ports Act, 1908 with a modern framework for port governance.

    It focuses on:

  • Integrated and evidence-based port development
  • Centre-State coordination
  • Strengthening State Maritime Boards
  • Dispute resolution
  • Safety and security
  • Pollution prevention
  • Digitalisation and ease of doing business

    • The Act also establishes the Maritime State Development Council as a statutory consultative mechanism between the Centre and coastal States.

    4. Bills of Lading Act, 2025

    A bill of lading is an important document in maritime trade that records the receipt and carriage of goods and establishes certain rights and obligations of the parties involved.

    The new Act modernises the legal framework governing bills of lading and seeks greater clarity regarding rights, liabilities and transfer of ownership.

    By reducing ambiguity and potential litigation, it aims to facilitate smoother and more efficient maritime commerce.

    5. Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025

    The Act replaces the earlier colonial-era framework governing the carriage of goods by sea.

    It retains the Hague-Visby Rules, helping maintain India's alignment with internationally recognised maritime practices.

    The legislation seeks to improve transparency, legal certainty and commercial efficiency in the transportation of goods by sea.

    Why Are These Reforms Significant?

    The five Acts represent more than a change in maritime legislation. They indicate a broader shift towards developing India as a competitive maritime and logistics hub.

    Their potential significance includes:

  • Lower logistics costs: Greater use of coastal shipping and efficient ports can improve freight movement.
  • Trade competitiveness: Modern maritime laws can facilitate smoother international trade.
  • Blue Economy: Better utilisation of maritime resources can support sustainable economic growth.
  • Ease of doing business: Simplified regulations can encourage private investment.
  • Employment: Expansion of shipping, ports, shipbuilding and maritime services can generate jobs.
  • Environmental sustainability: Greater emphasis on pollution prevention and greener transport can support sustainable development.
  • Strategic importance: A stronger domestic maritime ecosystem can enhance India's economic and strategic presence in the Indian Ocean Region.

    • Challenges

    The effectiveness of these reforms will depend on implementation. India needs continued investment in port infrastructure, multimodal connectivity, shipbuilding, maritime technology and skilled manpower.

    Coordination between the Centre, States, port authorities and private stakeholders will also be essential. At the same time, maritime expansion must balance economic objectives with marine environmental protection and pollution control.

    Way Forward

    India's maritime strategy needs to move beyond ports alone towards an integrated ecosystem covering shipping, coastal transport, inland waterways, logistics, shipbuilding, maritime services and environmental sustainability.

    Effective implementation of the new laws, combined with infrastructure development and technological modernisation, can help India strengthen its maritime capabilities and realise the objectives of Maritime Vision 2047 and Viksit Bharat 2047.

currentAffairs.Title: BRICS, De-Dollarisation & Global Trade: Can BRICS Reshape the Global Economic Order?
currentAffairs.Category: GS II - International Relations | GS III - Economy
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: Explore BRICS’ expanding economic influence, de-dollarisation efforts, global trade, intra-BRICS competition, cross-border payments, and its potential to reshape the global economic order.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Syllabus Areas:

GS II - International Relations | GS III - Economy

BRICS has expanded its membership and now represents a larger share of the global economy in PPP (Purchasing Power Parity) terms than G7. The bloc is a forum for multipolarity and shared prosperity.

But, BRICS countries are causing inflation, losses of export revenues and growth stagnation to their partners.

For instance, its $100-billion Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA) established in 2014, provides balance-of-payments support during financial stress. But the CRA does not monitor or coordinate the currency, commodity and inflation spillovers members impose on one another.

BRICS therefore has crisis-response tools but no comparable surveillance mechanism.

Nearly two decades on, BRICS has no common mechanism for members to discuss economic damage arising from other members' policies.

So it has ended up as an economic family without the family spirit needed for solidarity. The consequences of this institutional gap are already visible in how members' domestic economic decisions spill across BRICS borders.

Among the members of BRICS+, several major exporters compete in overlapping markets. This creates structural conflicts of interest among members in their export strategies.

This contradiction became evident when Saudi Arabia and the UAE joined BRICS in 2024, making the group home to three major oil producers. The discounted oil offered by Russia from 2022 is illustrative of how one member can defend market share at the cost of another.

This spillover can also be evident in imports.

  • India imports up to $132 billion of goods a year from China, which is a major channel for Chinese cost pressures to enter the Indian economy.
  • Rising production costs in China, whether due to wages, energy or supply disruptions, can increase costs for Indian importers, which can trickle down to domestic prices. But BRICS has not measured nor addressed these externalities of inflation.

    • 18th summit of BRICS - Theme:

    "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" holds relevance in a context of globally fraught geopolitics.

    The group's name is an offshoot of the term BRIC coined by British economist Jim O'Neill and popularised by Goldman Sachs as shorthand for four vibrant markets Brazil, Russia, India, China. That they banded together and were joined by South Africa and later by Egypt, Iran, Ethiopia, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Indonesia testifies to the global need for a broad non-Western forum.

    Reducing global dependence on the U.S. dollar

    Reducing global dependence on the U.S. dollar is a key part of the discussions in the 18th BRICS Summit, scheduled to be held in India, happening in New Delhi from September 12 and 13, 2026.

    De-dollarization is the process of reducing dependence on the US dollar in international trade, finance, reserves, and cross-border transactions globally.

    Finance ministers and central bank governors from BRICS countries, under India’s chairmanship, will meet from August to discuss the facilitation of cross-border payments and strengthening of national currencies.

    Present Payment Method:

  • Currently, making payments across countries involves correspondent banking networks, with each country holding accounts with each other.
  • In countries where such correspondent banks do not have arrangements with each other, the transactions are routed through international banks, converting the currency of the sender into dollars, and then converting the dollars to the currency of the recipient country.
  • This process, besides being slow at times, comes with the cost of foreign exchange margins and the fee charged by the intermediaries.

    • Seeing that the BRICS comprises many developing economies, this can be among the many impediments to trade opportunities.

    Iran depends on BRICS for more than 65% of its imports, and Ethiopia nearly 45%. Intra-BRICS import dependency could be on the rise due to the heterogeneous composition of goods available among its members, as pointed out in a report by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development.

    Conversely, the dependency within the bloc has also risen. In the last decade, five members (Russia, India, China, Brazil, and Indonesia) have doubled and even quadrupled their exports to other BRICS countries. However, China has consistently shown the lowest dependency on the intra-BRICS export market.

  • Russia saw a rapid increase in its export dependency between 2020 and 2023, in the middle of its invasion of Ukraine, during which countries such as India imported more of its fuel.
  • The country saw a decline in export dependence in 2024. It was under Russia’s chairmanship in 2024 that the BRICS argued against the dominance of the U.S. dollar.
  • Russia was hit directly by the dollar monopoly in 2022, due to sanctions from the U.S. Russian banks were cut off from the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunications (SWIFT), which enables institutions to settle amounts. Hence, international transactions proved difficult for Russia.

    • While the U.S. is the largest economy in the world, the BRICS bloc does not fall far behind, as China, India, and Russia are in the top 10 in terms of Gross Domestic Product (current prices). Whether this collective economic strength can challenge the dominance of the dollar is to be seen in the coming days.

currentAffairs.Category:

GS-III: Infrastructure
currentAffairs.Short_Summary:

It examines issues of human rights, child safety, access to education, and accountability in public infrastructure development
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
“Bridging the Gap: Infrastructure, Human Rights and Last-Mile Governance”

Syllabus areas:

GS-II: Governance, Human Rights, Child Rights, Right to Education, Accountability

GS-III: Infrastructure, Project Implementation , Safety

Why in news?

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India has taken suo motu cognizance of a media report that dozens of children from Khambhatha and nearby settlements in the Mainpur Block area of Gariyaband district in Chhattisgarh, are compelled to climb a narrow and slippery iron ladder, attached to an unfinished bridge, to cross the Paiririver to reach their schools. Reportedly, the monsoon turns the shallow river into a torrent.

The Commission has observed that the contents of the media report, if true, raise serious issues of violation of human rights. Therefore, it has issued a notice to the Chief Secretary, Government of Chhattisgarh, calling for a detailed report on the matter within two weeks.

According to the media report, carried on 3rd September 2026, a roughly 300-metre-long bridge between Deharguda and Khambhatha in Mainpur Block has been under construction for nearly six years despite the villagers having been assured of its completion in six months by the concerned authorities about a year ago.

A Case of Basic Infrastructure Failure

  • School children being forced to cross a river through an unfinished bridge.
  • Bridge under construction for nearly six years.
  • Risks to children's life, safety, education and dignity.
  • Disconnect between infrastructure expenditure and actual service delivery.

    • What is NHRC?

    The National Human Rights Commission is a statutory body established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. It is mandated to protect and promote human rights.

    However, the NHRC's recommendations are generally recommendatory rather than equivalent to binding judicial orders. Ultimately, effective remedial action depends upon responsible administration and implementation by the concerned authorities.

    Infrastructure as a Human Rights Enabler

    Infrastructure is often viewed primarily from an economic perspective. However, its social and rights-based dimensions are equally important. A bridge can connect villages to schools, hospitals, markets and government institutions. Its absence can isolate communities and restrict access to essential services.

    In the Gariyaband case, the unfinished bridge is not simply an example of delayed public works. If children are compelled to undertake a dangerous journey to reach school, the infrastructure deficit directly affects their ability to exercise basic rights.

    This demonstrates an important principle of governance: the availability of a public service does not necessarily mean that people have meaningful access to it.

    Child Rights Perspective

    Children are among the most vulnerable sections of society and require special protection from avoidable risks.

    When children have to cross a river using an unfinished or unsafe structure, their physical safety is placed at risk. Such circumstances can also affect school attendance and educational continuity.

    The principle of the best interests of the child should therefore guide public policy decisions affecting children's access to education and essential services.

    Infrastructure projects near schools or along frequently used routes should incorporate child-safety considerations during planning, construction and monitoring.

    Governance and Administrative Accountability

    A major concern arising from the incident is the prolonged delay in completing the bridge.

    Public infrastructure projects can face delays because of several factors, including:

  • Poor project planning
  • Contractual disputes
  • Funding constraints
  • Land or statutory issues
  • Weak project monitoring
  • Administrative coordination failures
  • Contractor-related problems
  • Lack of timely corrective action

    • The precise reasons in this particular case need to be established through the official inquiry.

    Nevertheless, the broader governance lesson is clear: accountability should not end with sanctioning a project. Authorities must ensure timely execution, quality control, safety and eventual functionality.

    Education Requires More Than Schools

    The incident also highlights the need to look beyond school enrolment when assessing educational outcomes.

    A functional education system requires:

  • Accessible schools
  • Safe roads and bridges
  • Transportation facilities where necessary
  • Electricity and digital connectivity
  • Drinking water and sanitation
  • Adequate teachers and learning resources

    • Thus, education policy must be supported by infrastructure and connectivity policies.

    This calls for greater convergence among departments dealing with education, rural development, roads, public works and disaster management.

    Way Forward

    Several measures can address such infrastructure and governance gaps:

    1. Immediate safety arrangements: A safe temporary route should be provided until the permanent bridge is completed.

    2. Time-bound completion: Delayed projects should have clearly defined milestones and periodic review mechanisms.

    3. Strong project monitoring: Technology such as geo-tagging, digital dashboards and milestone-based monitoring can improve transparency.

    4. Fixing responsibility: Where avoidable administrative or contractual failures are established, appropriate accountability should follow.

    5. Child-centred planning: Infrastructure projects affecting children's mobility should include specific safety assessments.

    6. Community participation: Local communities can play an important role in monitoring public works and reporting deficiencies.

    7. Inter-departmental coordination: Education, infrastructure, rural development and disaster-management authorities should coordinate wherever infrastructure affects access to essential services.

    8. Outcome-based evaluation: Projects should ultimately be assessed on whether they provide safe, accessible and reliable public services.

currentAffairs.Title: Domestic Workers: Legal Protection
currentAffairs.Category: GS Paper I, GS Paper III, GS Paper IV - Human Dignity, Social Justice, Essay - Dignity of Labour
currentAffairs.Short_Summary:
This article examines the challenges faced by domestic workers and the need for comprehensive legal protection, social security, and fair working conditions.
It highlights key laws, welfare measures, ILO provisions, and initiatives aimed at safeguarding the rights and dignity of domestic workers.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Domestic Workers: Legal Protection

Syllabus areas:

GS Paper I - Indian Society, Role of Women, Vulnerable Sections, Social Empowerment, Migration and Informal Employment

GS Paper III – Employment, Informal/Unorganised Sector, Labour Reforms, Inclusive Growth, Social Security

GS Paper IV - Human Dignity, Social Justice, Compassion, Accountability, Ethical Treatment of Vulnerable Workers

Essay - Dignity of Labour, Women Empowerment, Social Security, Inclusive Development, Rights of Informal Workers, Social Justice

Domestic Workers

The Supreme Court directed Union Government to enact comprehensive law to stipulate the rights of domestic workers and set up a committee for framework on this. Even the court directed to submit the committee report in 6 months but in vain.

India has 40 million to 90 million domestic workers, majority of them are women and girls. Most of them are SC, ST. These workers may face harassment, abuse etc. Child labour is rampant.

Domestic workers may be:

1. live-in workers residing in employer's home

2. Live – out workers commuting daily.

Exploitative Employment Agencies and Brokers

Many domestic workers are migrant workers even from neighbouring countries, not only from another state.

Their contribution to global economy is recognised by the International Labour Organisation (ILO), hence passed Convention in 2011 to ensure the rights and protections of domestic workers.

While India voted in favour of this, it is yet to ratify it.

Interestingly, multiple attempts to pass such legislations since 1950.

The National Platform for Domestic Workers formed in 2012. It drafted Domestic Workers (Regulation of Work and Social Security) Bill in 2017.

State-Level Initiatives

Tamil Nadu Govt set up welfare board under Tamil Nadu Manual Workers Act, 1982.

Under this, minimum wage of 39 Rupees per hour.

Karnataka Govt announced introduction of Domestic Workers (Social Security and Welfare) Bill, 2025.

In India only 12 states stipulate minimum wage for domestic workers.

Examples: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala, Telangana etc.

→ All South India states

Legal Framework

  • Unorganised Workers Social Security Act, 2008
  • Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition, Redressal) Act, 2013
  • ILO Convention (189) – 2011 – yet to be ratified
  • Minimum Wages Act, 1948

    • Organisations and Movements

  • National Domestic Workers Movement
  • Self Employed Women's Association
  • All India Domestic Workers Union
  • National Platform for Domestic Workers

currentAffairs.Category: GS Paper I – Geography GS Paper III – Indian Economy
currentAffairs.Short_Summary:
Explore India’s Dedicated Freight Corridors and understand how dedicated rail infrastructure enables faster freight movement, efficient logistics and reduced transportation costs.
Learn about their routes, significance, economic impact and role in strengthening India’s supply-chain and infrastructure network.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
FREIGHT CORRIDORS IN INDIA

Transforming India's Logistics and Transport Infrastructure

Syllabus areas:

GS Paper I – Geography

GS Paper III – Indian Economy

Why in the news?

On 8 September 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the final three sections of the Western Dedicated Freight Corridor (WDFC) in Gujarat–Maharashtra. These sections cover 326 km and complete the entire 1,506-km WDFC from Dadri to JNPT. It is the 2nd major operational Dedicated Freight Corridor in India — the Western DFC (WDFC). The first one is Easternal.

India's principal DFC network comprises major corridors.

A. Eastern Dedicated Freight Corridor — EDFC

Route: Ludhiana → Sonnagar Length: approximately 1,337 km

It primarily serves the movement of heavy freight associated with sectors such as coal, steel and other industries, connecting northern hinterlands with the eastern industrial belt.

B. Western Dedicated Freight Corridor — WDFC

Route: Dadri → Jawaharlal Nehru Port (JNPT) Length: approximately 1,506 km

It connects the northern hinterland with important industrial regions of western India and provides connectivity towards JNPT, an important container port.

The combined length of the two corridors is approximately 2,843 km.

Additional corridors: proposed/planned and at different stages of DPR/preparation.

1. East Coast DFC — Kharagpur–Vijayawada — proposed/DPR stage.

2. East–West DFC — Palghar–Dankuni and associated sections — proposed/DPR stage.

3. North–South DFC — Vijayawada–Nagpur–Itarsi (with further proposed extension) — pr oposed/DPR stage.

4. Dankuni–Surat DFC — announced in Union Budget 2026; DPR preparation/updating is underway.

PM Modi described the dedicated freight corridor as the lifeline of a rapidly developing nation and also noted that India’s economic transformation was accelerating due to the modern freight structure.

Earlier, passenger and goods trains were forced to run on the same tracks, which severely hampered both passenger travel and freight movement, but the dedicated corridor altered that dynamic.

1. what is Freight corridor?

The movement of goods is the backbone of a modern economy. Raw materials have to move from mines and farms to factories, manufactured goods have to reach markets, and export commodities have to reach ports. Therefore, efficient freight transportation is essential for economic growth, industrialisation and international trade.

“India's freight transport is multimodal—road, rail, waterways and air—while Dedicated Freight Corridors specifically refer to dedicated railway infrastructure for freight movement.”

India has traditionally depended heavily on both road and rail networks for freight movement. However, conventional railway routes carry both passenger and freight trains. This creates congestion and limits the speed, capacity and reliability of goods transportation.

To address this problem, India has developed Dedicated Freight Corridors (DFCs)—special railway corridors designed primarily for the efficient movement of freight.

For roads, India has Economic Corridors, National Corridors, Inter-Corridors and Feeder Routes, mainly developed under Bharatmala Pariyojana.

2. Why Does India Need Freight Corridors?

India has one of the world's largest railway networks, but its conventional routes face heavy utilisation because passenger and freight trains share the same infrastructure.

A goods train may have to wait for passenger trains to pass, reducing its average speed and increasing transportation time.

The basic problem can be understood as:

Modes of Freight Transportation in India

1. Road Freight: Trucks and road networks are the most flexible mode for transporting goods, especially for short and medium distances.

2. Rail Freight: Railways are suitable for transporting large quantities of bulk goods over long distances at relatively lower costs.

3. Dedicated Freight Corridors (DFCs): Special railway corridors such as the Eastern and Western DFCs improve the speed and capacity of freight movement.

4. Water Freight: Inland waterways and coastal shipping are economical for transporting heavy and bulky commodities over long distances.

5. National Waterways: India uses designated waterways to facilitate inland freight movement through rivers and canals.

6. Coastal Shipping: Goods can be transported between Indian ports along the country's coastline.

7. Air Freight: Air cargo is mainly used for high-value, perishable and time-sensitive commodities because of its speed.

8. Multimodal Freight: Goods may move through a combination of road, rail, waterways and air during a single supply chain.

9. Road–Rail Integration: Trucks can transport goods to and from railway terminals, while trains handle the long-distance movement.

10. Port Connectivity: Roads and railways connect production centres and logistics hubs with major ports for international trade.

11. Logistics Parks and Terminals: These facilities enable storage, handling, consolidation and transfer of freight between different modes.

12. Economic Corridors: Road-based economic corridors improve connectivity between production centres, markets, ports and consumption centres.

13. Freight Networks: Together, these modes form an integrated network connecting agriculture, mining, manufacturing and markets.

14. Balanced Modal Mix: Greater use of rail and waterways can reduce pressure on roads, fuel consumption, congestion and logistics costs.

15. Way Forward: India's freight system is moving towards multimodal, integrated and technology-driven logistics for faster and more efficient movement of goods.
