currentAffairs.Title: Jute: India’s Golden Fibre
currentAffairs.Category: GS III - Economy, Agriculture, Environment
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: Explore jute sector of India, its historical evolution, farmer-focused policies, sustainable applications, technological innovations, market expansion, and growing role in green economic development.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Syllabus Areas:

GS III - Economy, Agriculture, Environment

Jute, widely known as India’s “Golden Fibre,” is an important natural fibre with applications ranging from packaging and textiles to agriculture, construction and environmental management. India remains the world’s largest producer of raw jute, and the sector supports millions of farmers, workers and entrepreneurs. Recent government interventions focus on improving productivity, farmer incomes, value addition, diversification and sustainable applications of jute.

Major characteristics of jute

  • Completely biodegradable and recyclable
  • Strong and durable
  • Breathable
  • Highly versatile
  • Thermal and acoustic insulation properties
  • Good moisture absorption
  • Blends easily with other fibres and wool
  • Relatively inexpensive compared with many other natural fibres

    • Importance to rural livelihoods

    The industry provides direct employment to approximately 3.70 lakh workers and indirectly supports the livelihoods of around 40 lakh farmers and their families, particularly in eastern and northeastern India.

    Major Jute-Producing Regions

    Jute cultivation is concentrated mainly in regions with suitable agro-climatic conditions.

    Major producing states

  • West Bengal
  • Bihar
  • Assam
  • Odisha
  • Andhra Pradesh
  • Jharkhand

    • West Bengal accounts for the largest share of raw jute cultivation in the country. The article notes that West Bengal alone has 89 of India’s 120 composite jute mills.

    Jute Geotextiles: Jute for Sustainable Infrastructure

    JGT is a versatile, diversified jute product belonging to the technical textiles category. It can be applied in many fields of civil engineering and environmental management.

    Why Jute Geotextiles are important

    Jute geotextiles are:

  • Fully biodegradable
  • Environmentally friendly
  • Economical
  • Technically effective
  • Suitable for soil stabilisation and erosion control

    • They help regulate the micro-environment, improve soil temperatures and support germination and early plant establishment.

    The government raised raw jute MSP to ₹5,925 per quintal in 2026–27, from ₹2,400 in 2014–15, a 147% increase, ensuring remunerative prices, reducing market risks, sustaining cultivation, livelihoods, and industry.

    Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory Use in Packing Commodities) Act:

    The Jute Packaging Materials Act promotes jute demand by mandating jute packaging for 100% of foodgrains and 20% of sugar, creating a stable domestic market while supporting jute farmers, mills, employment, and the industry’s sustainability.

    Jute Raw Material Bank (JRMB)

    The Jute Raw Material Bank (JRMB) facilitates the supply of raw jute materials to the unorganised sector, small production units and manufacturers of diversified jute products. By providing materials at economical prices, it supports artisans, women SHGs and MSMEs while promoting product diversification and sustaining rural livelihoods.

    Jute Mark India Logo

    The Jute Mark India initiative promotes authenticity, quality assurance and sustainability across jute products. The logo certifies compliance with quality standards and verifies jute content in labelled products. It strengthens consumer confidence, improves brand recognition and establishes a structured quality framework for India’s jute industry.

    Domestic Marketing and Jute Fairs

    The government promotes domestic jute consumption through regional jute fairs, with 57 fairs organised during FY 2025–26 across major cities. These fairs provide producers and entrepreneurs opportunities to display products, interact with buyers, expand markets, promote diversified jute products and increase consumer awareness.

    Overall Significance of the Jute Sector

  • Sustainable Growth: Promotes sustainable agriculture and environmental conservation through a biodegradable natural fibre.
  • Livelihoods: Supports farmers, rural communities and women SHGs.
  • Industrial Development: Strengthens MSMEs, technical textiles and diversified products.
  • Infrastructure: Expands jute applications in sustainable infrastructure.
  • Green Economy: Encourages jute as an alternative to plastics.
  • Technology: Integrates digital governance and remote sensing.
  • Global Markets: Promotes exports and market expansion through value addition.
  • Policy Approach: Combines farmer support, industrial development, innovation, sustainability and market development.

    • India's jute sector is evolving from a traditional fibre industry into a sustainable, diversified and technology-enabled ecosystem that simultaneously supports farmers, rural livelihoods, MSMEs, exports and environmental protection.

currentAffairs.Title: Vibrant Villages Programme (VVP)
currentAffairs.Category: GS I - Geography | GS III - Internal Security
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: Explore how the Vibrant Villages Programme transforms India’s border communities through development, connectivity, livelihoods, tourism, governance and strategic security, strengthening resilient frontiers.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Syllabus Areas:

GS I - Geography | GS III - Internal Security

The Vibrant Villages Programme (VVP) is a strategic development initiative aimed at transforming India’s border villages into vibrant, resilient and prosperous communities. The programme goes beyond conventional infrastructure development by linking border development with national security, livelihoods, connectivity, governance and community participation. It is being implemented through VVP-I and VVP-II, with a combined financial outlay of ₹11,639 crore.

Historically, many border villages faced:

  • Difficult terrain
  • Poor connectivity
  • Limited infrastructure
  • Inadequate livelihood opportunities
  • Restricted access to healthcare and education
  • Out-migration due to limited economic opportunities

    • This resulted in several frontier areas becoming sparsely populated.

    The VVP seeks to address these structural challenges by accelerating comprehensive development in strategically important border villages. Importantly, the programme changes the perception of these settlements—from being viewed as remote or peripheral areas to being treated as “the nation’s first” villages.

    The programme recognises border residents as the “eyes and ears” of the border, making thriving local communities an important component of national security.

    Strategic significance

    The importance of border communities is illustrated by the 1999 Kargil intrusion, when local residents were the first to report suspicious movements in the Kargil sector on 3 May 1999. This highlights how an alert and well-connected border population can contribute to the country's security.

    Two Phases of the Vibrant Villages Programme

    The programme is being implemented in two phases to progressively cover India's international land borders.

    The two phases share a common objective: improving living conditions, generating local livelihoods and empowering border communities, thereby making border villages vibrant centres of development and strengthening national security.

    VVP-I: Strengthening Northern Border Communities

  • Announced: Union Budget 2022-23; launched at Kibithoo, Arunachal Pradesh, on 10 April 2023.
  • Coverage: 662 strategic villages across Arunachal Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Ladakh, covering about 1.42 lakh people.
  • Village-wise: Arunachal Pradesh – 455; Himachal Pradesh – 75; Uttarakhand – 51; Sikkim – 46; Ladakh – 35.
  • Outlay: ₹4,800 crore (2022-23 to 2026-27), including ₹2,500 crore for roads.

    • Major Interventions

    Roads & connectivity • Drinking water • Electricity • Telecom • Healthcare • Education • Tourism • Livelihoods • Financial inclusion • Skill development • Women & youth empowerment • SHGs, cooperatives & FPOs • Local culture • One-Block-One-Product • Social entrepreneurship

    The programme follows a hub-and-spoke livelihood model and promotes convergence of government schemes for comprehensive border development.

    VVP-II: Extending the Model to All Land Borders

  • Approved: 2 April 2025; launched on 20 February 2026 at Nathonpur, Assam.
  • Nature: Central Sector Scheme, 100% Union Government-funded and implemented by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).
  • Outlay: ₹6,839 crore (2024-25 to 2028-29).
  • Coverage: 1,954 villages in 334 blocks across 15 States and 2 UTs.
  • Covers international land borders other than northern-border villages already covered under VVP-I.

    • Key Interventions

    Infrastructure • Roads • Healthcare • Financial inclusion • Skill development • Telecom • Tourism • Sustainable livelihoods • Cooperatives • SHGs • Local value chains • SMART classrooms

    Four Key Connectivity Areas

    All-weather roads • Television connectivity • Telecom connectivity • On-grid electrification

    Core objective: Improve living conditions, create livelihoods and encourage people to stay in border villages, thereby strengthening resilient frontier communities.

    Road Connectivity and Long-Span Bridges

    Connectivity is a major pillar of the programme because geographical isolation is one of the biggest constraints faced by remote border settlements.

    Under VVP-I:

  • 111 road projects were sanctioned.
  • These projects have an outlay of ₹2,481.93 crore.
  • They will connect 134 villages that previously lacked road connectivity.
  • 35 long-span bridges were also sanctioned.

    • Improved roads are expected to:

  • Reduce travel difficulties
  • Connect villages with markets
  • Improve access to essential services
  • Support tourism
  • Strengthen overall integration of remote villages with the wider economy

    • Youth Engagement: Viksit Vibrant Village Programme

    In 2026, the Viksit Vibrant Village Programme engaged 400+ volunteers from all States and UTs across 74 border villages in Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Volunteers contributed through community service, cultural exchange and grassroots development, helping youth understand India’s frontier regions while supporting local communities and development.

    VVP’s Impact Beyond Infrastructure

    A. Security

    Strong, populated and economically viable border communities support border forces while creating frontier populations that serve as strategic national assets.

    B. Demography & Reverse Migration

    Better connectivity and livelihoods encourage families to remain or return, helping reduce out-migration and demographic vulnerability in remote frontier areas.

    C. Local Economy

    Tourism, cooperatives, SHGs, FPOs and local enterprises create sustainable local incomes, while border-force procurement provides nearby markets for village producers.

    D. Governance

    Scheme convergence and Village Action Plans help eligible households access government schemes while enabling district administrations to coordinate departmental interventions.

    Border Development as a Security Strategy

    VVP links development with security: better services reduce migration, strengthen populations, expand local economies, build resilience and support border security.

    The Vibrant Villages Programme transforms border settlements into partners in development and national security. Through infrastructure, connectivity, livelihoods, tourism, healthcare, education and scheme convergence, it promotes prosperous, resilient communities, strengthens India’s borders, and advances the vision of a secure, inclusive Viksit Bharat by 2047.

    Also Read: Districts as Export Hubs

currentAffairs.Title: Geothermal Energy
currentAffairs.Category: GS I - Geography | GS III - Economy
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: Explore India’s geothermal potential, from Puga Valley’s first wells to national policy, global lessons, technological innovation, and pathways toward clean, secure energy and Net Zero 2070.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Syllabus Areas:

GS I - Geography | GS III - Economy

India is increasingly looking beyond conventional renewable sources such as solar and wind to build a reliable, low-carbon and diversified energy system. Geothermal energy—heat derived from the Earth’s interior—offers an important opportunity in this transition. The recent commissioning of India’s first two geothermal wells at Puga Valley in Ladakh marks a significant shift from geothermal resource assessment towards field-level demonstration.

Unlike solar and wind energy, geothermal energy does not depend directly on sunlight or wind conditions. This gives it an important role in providing a more stable renewable-energy mix

Deep wells bring naturally heated water or steam to the surface. The steam can drive a turbine connected to a generator. After electricity generation, the water can be condensed and reinjected into the geothermal reservoir, helping replenish the resource.

Why is the Earth Hot?

Earth’s interior contains enormous heat, which increases with depth.

  • Four layers: Crust → Mantle → Outer Core → Inner Core
  • Temperature: ~3,700°C at the mantle–core boundary; 5,000–6,000°C in the core.
  • Main sources of heat: Radioactive decay of uranium, thorium and potassium, plus residual heat from Earth’s formation.
  • This heat drives convection currents and, through geological faults and fractures, can bring hot fluids closer to the surface.
  • These processes create geothermal reservoirs of hot water and steam, which can be harnessed for energy.

    • Geothermal Energy: Electricity and Beyond

    Geothermal energy is used for electricity generation by converting underground hot water and steam into power. It also provides direct heat for district heating, agriculture, aquaculture, space heating, cooling, and other thermal applications, making it a versatile renewable energy source.

    Enhanced and Advanced Geothermal Systems

    India's geothermal potential is not limited to naturally accessible geothermal reservoirs.

    The article highlights emerging technologies such as:

    1. Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS)

    EGS can expand geothermal opportunities in areas where naturally occurring geothermal reservoirs may not be sufficiently productive.

    2. Advanced Geothermal Systems (AGS)

    AGS represents another technological pathway for accessing geothermal resources and broadening the geographical scope of geothermal development.

    These technologies could become increasingly important because India's geothermal potential is substantial, but commercially viable resources are not necessarily available everywhere in easily exploitable form.

    India’s Geothermal Demonstration Projects

    India is moving from resource assessment → field demonstration → technology development.

  • Ankleshwar, Gujarat: Geothermal power pilot using unproductive oil & gas wells.
  • Gandhinagar, Gujarat: Solar + geothermal project; 70–80°C fluid and 50–90 kW power demonstrated.
  • Tawang, Arunachal Pradesh: Geothermal resource assessment at 5 sites.
  • Hyderabad, Telangana: Research on geothermal cooling/air-conditioning.
  • Shallow Geothermal: Borehole Heat Exchangers for heating and cooling

    • National Policy on Geothermal Energy, 2025 🇮🇳

  • Notified in September 2025
  • Nodal Ministry: MNRE
  • Goal: Make geothermal energy a major renewable-energy pillar.
  • Focus: Exploration, R&D, drilling, reservoir management, GSHPs, direct use, abandoned-well reuse, pilot projects, data repository, Centres of Excellence, PPPs and skill development.

    • Geothermal Energy & Net Zero 2070

  • Supports energy security through diversification.
  • Complements solar and wind with relatively steady energy.
  • Helps advance low-carbon energy transition.
  • Supports India’s Net Zero 2070 goal.

    • International Cooperation

  • Australia & Iceland: Geothermal cooperation.
  • Saudi Arabia: Geothermal identified under bilateral engagement.
  • Benefits: Technology, expertise, research, best practices and capacity building.

    • RE-RTD Programme

    The Renewable Energy Research and Technology Development Programme (RE-RTD) is another component supporting technological development.

  • Implemented by MNRE with research institutions and industry.
  • Focuses on indigenous, cost-effective renewable-energy technologies, including geothermal.

    • Key Advantages of Geothermal Energy

  • 24/7 Availability – Provides steady energy with less dependence on weather.
  • Low Carbon – Cleaner alternative to fossil fuels.
  • Renewable – Can provide long-term energy when properly managed.
  • Multiple Uses – Electricity, heating, cooling, agriculture and aquaculture.
  • Energy Security – Indigenous resource that can reduce fossil-fuel dependence.
  • Supports Other Renewables – Complements variable sources like solar and wind.

    • Key Challenges

  • Geological uncertainty – Not every identified resource is commercially viable.
  • High exploration costs & risk – Deep drilling requires major investment.
  • Technology gaps – EGS/AGS may be needed for difficult resources.
  • Limited field experience – India is still developing technical expertise and data.
  • No commercial-scale power generation yet – Converting potential into economically viable projects remains the key challenge.

    • Geothermal energy should be treated as a strategic complement to India's solar, wind, hydro and other renewable resources, helping create a more diversified and resilient clean-energy system.

currentAffairs.Title: Rising Dam Levels Across India
currentAffairs.Category: GS I - Geography | GS II - Governance | GS III - Environment
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: India’s reservoir storage shows regional gains despite deficient monsoon rainfall, highlighting water availability, irrigation needs, regional disparities, and the importance of sustainable reservoir management.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Syllabus Areas:

GS I - Geography

GS II - Governance

GS III - Environment

India’s reservoir storage is in focus amid a deficient monsoon, with Central and Western regions exceeding 80% capacity, while overall storage remains below last year’s level and the 10-year average.

Also Read: Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari (JSJB)

What is a Reservoir?

A reservoir is a large, artificial or natural storage area used to collect and store water, usually created by building a dam across a river.

  • 30%+ of 166 major reservoirs have storage above 80% of capacity.
  • South-West monsoon was 13% deficient as of September 3.
  • 47% of 734 districts received deficient rainfall.
  • 13 reservoirs were full, including 5 in Maharashtra; 51 remained below 50% capacity.
  • Continued rainfall in the coming days may further improve reservoir storage.
  • Central (81.2%) and Western (80.4%) regions recorded the highest storage levels.
  • Overall reservoir storage stood at 56.76%, or 129.87 BCM of 183.565 BCM capacity.
  • 4 of 5 regions had storage above 60%, but Southern storage declined.
  • Overall storage remained below both last year’s level and the 10-year average.

currentAffairs.Title: Himalayas’ Preparedness for GLOFs and Snow Avalanches
currentAffairs.Category: GS III - Disaster Management
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: A disaster-management perspective on Himalayan preparedness for GLOFs and snow avalanches, highlighting early warning, preventive mitigation, community resilience, evacuation and coordinated response mechanisms.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Syllabus Areas:

GS III - Disaster Management

Read Recent Disaster in Himalayas

The Himalayan region requires anticipatory, risk-informed disaster management for GLOFs and snow avalanches. On 3 September 2026, the Union Home Secretary reviewed preparedness, focusing on monitoring, early warning, evacuation, preventive mitigation, community preparedness and coordinated response across vulnerable Himalayan States/UTs.

Read About GLOF

The Key Shift: From Disaster Response to Disaster Risk Reduction

The most important takeaway is the government's emphasis on moving beyond a response-oriented approach.

Traditionally, disaster management tends to become visible after an extreme event—through rescue, relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction. However, disasters in fragile mountain environments can evolve rapidly, leaving very little time for emergency response.

Therefore, the focus needs to shift towards:

The recent review explicitly emphasised risk-informed planning, preventive mitigation and community-level preparedness.

This represents an important evolution in India's disaster-management approach: the objective is not merely to respond faster, but to reduce the probability and impact of disasters beforehand.

From Risk Identification to Resilient Response

Continuous & Proactive Risk Monitoring

Continuously monitor vulnerable glacial lakes, snow-covered and avalanche-prone areas, high-risk locations and flood flow paths, especially during heightened-risk periods. Strengthen coordination among scientific institutions, technical agencies and local administrations.

Last-Mile Connectivity

Ensure alerts reach remote villages, vulnerable settlements, downstream communities, local authorities and response teams. Technology must be supported by reliable local communication and community participation.

Evacuation Preparedness

Warnings are effective only when people can evacuate quickly and safely. Preparedness should identify vulnerable areas, evacuation routes, shelters, responsible authorities and emergency response arrangements.

Flow-Path Planning

Map potential flood-flow paths to identify exposed settlements and infrastructure, enabling better evacuation, response and resource positioning. Risk mapping must translate into action mapping.

District & Local-Level Implementation

Convert policies into location-specific actions, as Himalayan vulnerabilities vary across regions. Effective preparedness requires:

National framework → State strategy → District planning → Community action.

Major Governance Challenges

The recent review also highlights several broader challenges that India needs to address:

1. Last-mile warning gap: Scientific warnings must reach vulnerable communities quickly and in an actionable form.

2. Implementation gap: Preparedness plans need to translate into concrete district- and village-level actions.

3. Coordination gap: Multiple agencies generate and use risk information, making institutional coordination essential.

4. Evacuation gap: Warning without clearly planned evacuation can fail to prevent loss of life.

5. Monitoring gap: High-risk glacial lakes and avalanche-prone areas require continuous rather than occasional monitoring.

6. Community preparedness gap: Local populations need to be integrated into disaster-risk reduction rather than treated merely as beneficiaries.

7. Preventive mitigation gap: Investment should increasingly focus on reducing risk before disasters occur.

These challenges explain why the latest review emphasised proactive monitoring, preventive mitigation, community preparedness and regular plan reviews.

Way Forward

A resilient Himalayan disaster-management framework should focus on the following:

1. Strengthen end-to-end early warning: Develop systems that connect hazard detection with rapid warning dissemination and community action.

2. Improve last-mile communication: Combine technological systems with reliable local communication mechanisms for remote communities.

3. Make evacuation plans operational: Prepare location-specific evacuation routes, shelters, responsibilities and emergency protocols.

4. Strengthen district-level disaster governance: Ensure that national and State-level risk assessments translate into actionable district and local plans.

5. Institutionalise community participation: Conduct regular awareness programmes, preparedness exercises and community-level drills.

6. Promote multi-agency coordination: Enable seamless information sharing among MHA, NDMA, CWC, IMD, DGRE, State agencies, district administrations and scientific institutions.

7. Adopt a multi-hazard approach: Integrate preparedness for GLOFs, avalanches and other Himalayan hazards rather than treating each hazard in isolation.

8. Prioritise preventive mitigation: Move resources and planning towards reducing exposure and vulnerability before an extreme event occurs.

9. Regularly stress-test preparedness: Preparedness plans should be periodically reviewed, gaps identified and corrective measures implemented.

10. Expedite ongoing mitigation initiatives: Projects already sanctioned for GLOF mitigation should be implemented efficiently and monitored for outcomes.

The Himalayan disaster challenge is not simply about the occurrence of natural hazards; it is about how effectively institutions, infrastructure and communities are prepared to deal with them.

The real test of disaster management will therefore not be how quickly the government responds after a GLOF or avalanche, but how effectively it can anticipate risk, communicate warnings, evacuate vulnerable populations and reduce exposure before the disaster strikes.

For the Himalayan region, resilience must become a continuous process—not an emergency response activated after a disaster.

Mains Questions:

Q. “Disaster management in the Himalayan region needs to move from a response-centric approach to a risk-informed and community-based preparedness framework.” Discuss.

currentAffairs.Title: Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari (JSJB)
currentAffairs.Category: GS II - Governance | GS III - Environment
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari promotes community-led water conservation through rainwater harvesting, groundwater recharge, local ownership, scientific planning, and sustainable water-management practices for long-term water security.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Syllabus Areas:

GS II - Governance | GS III - Economy

The Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari (JSJB) initiative has expanded its focus from local water-conservation interventions to a broader national movement for water security through community participation.

The initiative was launched on 6 September 2024 with the objective of placing community partnership and ownership at the centre of water conservation. It promotes low-cost groundwater recharge and water-storage structures, revival of defunct borewells and locally appropriate solutions through a Whole-of-Government and Whole-of-Society approach.

National Focus on Water Conservation

The Ministry of Jal Shakti Departmental Summit was held in New Delhi on 1–2 September 2026.

It was the first in a series of Departmental Summits aimed at strengthening:

  • Cooperative federalism
  • Centre–State collaboration
  • Water governance
  • Inter-governmental coordination

    • Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari: Catch the Rain was one of the summit's four key thematic areas.

    The other areas included:

  • Water infrastructure projects
  • Source sustainability of drinking-water systems
  • Rural water supply under Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0

    • The summit linked water governance with the broader vision of a Water Secure India and Viksit Bharat 2047.

    Importance of Jan Bhagidari

  • Community participation & local ownership are central to sustainable water conservation.
  • Involves Panchayats, institutions and individuals through collective action.
  • Combines traditional knowledge, scientific planning and institutional support.
  • Aims to transform water conservation from a government programme into a people's movement.

    • Government Suggestions for Water Governance

  • Jal Utsav: Increase public awareness on water conservation.
  • Capacity Building: Strengthen water-management knowledge in universities and higher institutions.
  • Inter-State Study Visits: Enable officials, farmers and public representatives to replicate successful practices.
  • Water Data Governance: Integrate, systematically manage, analyse and effectively use water-sector data.

    • Broader Significance

  • JSJB shifts water security beyond infrastructure creation toward a culture of responsibility.
  • By placing Jan Bhagidari at its core, it integrates traditional knowledge, scientific planning, local ownership and institutional support, linking individual action with collective outcomes to build resilient communities and strengthen India’s water security.

    • Water Conservation in India:

    Water conservation in India is essential because the country faces increasing water scarcity due to rapid population growth, urbanization, industrialization, climate change, and overuse of groundwater. Conserving water helps ensure a sustainable supply for agriculture, industries, and households while protecting ecosystems.

    Importance of Water Conservation

  • Ensures availability of water for future generations.
  • Supports agriculture, which consumes nearly 80% of India's freshwater.
  • Reduces the impact of droughts and water shortages.
  • Protects rivers, lakes, and groundwater resources.
  • Improves public health by ensuring access to clean water.

currentAffairs.Title: Cultivation of Kalanamak Rice
currentAffairs.Category: GS III - Economy - Agriculture
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: Kalanamak rice highlights how traditional crop conservation, improved varieties, government support, value addition, farmer empowerment, and export promotion can transform agriculture and livelihoods.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Cultivation of Kalanamak Rice

Syllabus Areas:

GS III - Economy - Agriculture

Kalanamak rice, a traditional aromatic rice variety associated particularly with Siddharthnagar district of Uttar Pradesh, has witnessed significant growth in cultivation, productivity, farmer participation, processing and market opportunities in recent years. The government is supporting the crop through financial assistance, improved varieties, seed production, processing infrastructure, branding and export promotion.

Significant Growth in Kalanamak Rice Cultivation

Kalanamak rice cultivation has expanded considerably in recent years, accompanied by improvements in productivity and farmer income.

Why it matters

The growth of Kalanamak demonstrates how a traditional crop can be converted into a higher-value agricultural commodity through better varieties, branding, processing, market access and government support.

Government Support for Kalanamak Farmers

Both the Central Government and State Government are providing financial, technical and marketing support to Kalanamak rice farmers.

One District One Product (ODOP) Initiative

Kalanamak has also been promoted through the One District One Product (ODOP) framework.

Important initiatives

  • The ODOP Margin Money Scheme provides support for eligible Kalanamak-related enterprises.
  • A Common Facility Centre (CFC) for Kalanamak rice has been established in Siddharthnagar.
  • The CFC provides local farmers with modern facilities for:
  • Processing
  • Packaging
  • Export support

    • The State Government has also earmarked dedicated project funding for the promotion, production and processing of Kalanamak rice.

    Significance

    This reflects a shift from merely increasing agricultural production towards developing an integrated value chain:

    Cultivation → Processing → Packaging → Branding → Marketing → Export

    Read Full Article on Districts as Export Hubs

    Research & Development of Improved Kalanamak Varieties

  • ICAR/National Agricultural Research System works on developing and conserving Kalanamak varieties.
  • Six improved varieties have been released:
  • Kalanamak KN3
  • Bauna Kalanamak 101
  • Bauna Kalanamak 102
  • Kalanamak Kiran
  • Pusa Narendra Kalanamak 1
  • Pusa CRD Kalanamak 2
  • The last two are dwarf, high-yielding varieties.
  • Average yield: Improved varieties – 4.5 tonnes/ha vs traditional varieties – 2.5 tonnes/ha.
  • KVKs in the Kalanamak GI area conduct multi-location testing of new varieties.
  • Focus: Higher yield + Climate resilience + Local suitability before wider release.

    • Conservation of Traditional Kalanamak Varieties

  • ICAR institutes and KVKs help farmers register and conserve traditional Kalanamak varieties under PPVFRA, protecting agricultural biodiversity and rice genetic resources, with over 1,700 varieties registered.

    • Quality Seed Production

  • Under the Breeder Seed Programme, 15–20 quintals of Kalanamak breeder seed are produced annually. During 2021–22 to 2025–26, 389.6 quintals were distributed to farmers.

    • Promotion in International Markets

  • APEDA promotes Kalanamak exports by linking FPOs with international buyers, facilitating shipments and market access, particularly to Singapore and Nepal, thereby strengthening agricultural export opportunities.

    • Agri-Export Zone Framework

    Siddharthnagar and surrounding Terai districts have been integrated into APEDA's Agri-Export Zone framework for specialty rice.

    This integration is intended to support:

  • Export packaging
  • Residue testing
  • Compliance with international requirements
  • Financial assistance for export-related activities

    • The approach helps create an ecosystem for taking specialty agricultural products from the farm to international markets.

    Importance of Kalanamak Rice for Agriculture

    The developments highlighted in the article demonstrate several broader agricultural themes.

  • Higher farmer profitability: The increase in the sale price from ₹40/kg to ₹150/kg has substantially improved profitability compared with ordinary rice.
  • Crop diversification: Kalanamak provides an opportunity to diversify beyond conventional rice cultivation and develop a specialty/high-value rice segment.
  • Value addition: Government support for processing and milling allows farmers and FPOs to participate in activities beyond cultivation.
  • Conservation of indigenous varieties: The conservation of traditional Kalanamak varieties helps protect agricultural biodiversity and traditional knowledge.
  • Climate-resilient agriculture: Testing new varieties for high yield and climate resilience indicates an attempt to make the crop more suitable for changing climatic conditions.
  • Export-oriented agriculture: Linking FPOs with international buyers and integrating the region into an Agri-Export Zone can strengthen India's agricultural export value chain.

    • Kalanamak rice showcases how conserving traditional varieties, ensuring quality seeds, strengthening processing, and promoting exports can enhance farmer incomes while preserving agricultural heritage and supporting sustainable growth.

currentAffairs.Title: Districts as Export Hubs
currentAffairs.Category: GS II - Governance | GS III - Economy
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: India’s Districts as Export Hubs initiative shifts focus from local production to global markets, strengthening MSMEs, exports, employment, competitiveness, and inclusive district-led economic growth.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Districts as Export Hubs

Syllabus Areas:

GS II - Governance | GS III - Economy

Watch the Video on District’s GDP

India’s export growth is entering a new phase—moving beyond traditional industrial centres to unlock the potential of every district, empower local producers, strengthen MSMEs, and integrate them with global markets.

Why India Needed a District-Led Export Model

  • Exports have become a key engine of India's growth story. Every rupee earned from overseas markets adds to jobs, incomes and industry at home.
  • India's total exports of goods and services touched an all-time high of US$ 825.25 billion in 2024-25, growing further to an estimated US$ 863.11 billion in 2025-26.
  • For decades, export activity stayed concentrated around a handful of established industrial clusters and port cities.
  • Small towns, rural districts and remote regions rarely found their way into shipment manifests, even though many held unique, high-quality products.
  • Products such as Bastar's iron craft, Jalgaon's bananas and Meghalaya's Mandarin Oranges reflected this untapped strength.
  • Recognising this opportunity, the Government brought in a district-led export strategy in the form of Districts as Export Hubs Initiative, enabling every district to contribute to India's export growth by leveraging its unique strengths.

    • The story of DEH begins with the One District One Product (ODOP) programme. ODOP set out to select, brand and promote one distinctive product from each district, converting local identity into economic opportunity.

    To strengthen this approach, the Department of Commerce through the DEH initiative under the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) has expanded the focus from product promotion to a comprehensive export promotion and ecosystem strengthening. As on January 2026, the DEH initiative covers more than 770 districts across the country, reflecting its expanding reach and stronger integration with overall export planning.

    Mapping products and services

    DEH identifies export-worthy products and services across districts. These include GI-tagged products, agricultural clusters, and toy clusters, engineering goods etc. District-specific mapping helps prepare targeted export strategies. Some of the products with export potential include:

currentAffairs.Title: Semicon 2.0
currentAffairs.Category: GS III - Economy | Science and Technology
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: Semicon 2.0 strengthens India’s semiconductor ecosystem through end-to-end capabilities, fiscal support, monitoring, domestic manufacturing, advanced R&D, and skilled talent development.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Semicon 2.0

Syllabus Areas:

GS III - Economy | Science and Technology

The Union Cabinet has approved Semicon 2.0 to strengthen India’s semiconductor design and manufacturing ecosystem. The initiative covers all six pillars, focusing on design, manufacturing, R&D, packaging and talent development.

What is Semicon?

Semicon is short for Semiconductor. A semiconductor is a material whose electrical conductivity lies between a conductor and an insulator and can be controlled to regulate the flow of electricity. Silicon is the most widely used semiconductor.

Major Applications

  • Computers: Processors, memory and GPUs
  • Smartphones: Processors, sensors and communication chips
  • Automobiles: EVs, sensors and control systems
  • AI: AI processors and accelerators
  • Telecom: 4G/5G and networking
  • Space & Defence: Radar, satellites and avionics
  • Energy: Solar systems, inverters and power electronics
  • Healthcare: Medical equipment and sensors
  • Industry & IoT: Automation, robotics and smart devices

    • Why are Semiconductors Important?

    Semiconductors are foundational to modern technologies and are essential for sectors such as:

  • Artificial Intelligence
  • Electronics and computing
  • Telecommunications
  • Automobiles
  • Defence and strategic technologies
  • Consumer electronics
  • Advanced manufacturing

    • Therefore, domestic semiconductor capabilities are important not only from an economic perspective, but also from the standpoint of national security and strategic autonomy.

    Key Achievements Highlighted

  • 85,000 Semiconductor Engineers: India developed 85,000 semiconductor engineers in four years, significantly ahead of the original 10-year target.
  • New Target: 1 Lakh Engineers: A new target has been set to develop another 1 lakh semiconductor engineers.
  • 250+ Chips Designed: Students from Tier-II and Tier-III cities have already designed more than 250 semiconductor chips.

    • This highlights the expansion of semiconductor capabilities beyond major metropolitan and technology centres.

    Strategic Significance for India

    1. Economic Growth: A stronger semiconductor ecosystem can support electronics manufacturing and high-tech industrial growth.

    2. Supply-Chain Resilience: Domestic capabilities can reduce vulnerability to disruptions in global semiconductor supply chains.

    3. National Security: Semiconductors are critical to strategic and security-related technologies, making domestic capabilities important for national security.

    4. Technological Leadership: Investment in design and advanced R&D can help India move towards higher-value segments of the technology ecosystem.

    5. Employment Generation: The ecosystem is expected to generate 50,000–60,000 direct jobs.

    6. Human Capital: The accelerated development of semiconductor engineers strengthens India's specialised technology workforce.

    Key Challenges

    While the source focuses primarily on the Government's initiatives and achievements, the broader implementation of such an ecosystem will require sustained attention to:

  • High capital requirements of semiconductor fabrication
  • Access to specialised equipment and materials
  • Advanced R&D capabilities
  • Availability of highly skilled manpower
  • Integration across the entire semiconductor value chain
  • Global competitiveness
  • Long gestation periods for advanced semiconductor projects

    • Way Forward

    India's semiconductor strategy should focus on:

  • Building the complete semiconductor value chain, from design to packaging.
  • Strengthening domestic R&D in advanced semiconductor technologies.
  • Deepening industry–academia collaboration.
  • Expanding semiconductor education and training beyond major cities.
  • Developing a reliable ecosystem for machines, materials and specialised inputs.
  • Encouraging private-sector participation and long-term investment.
  • Focusing on high-value semiconductor design and intellectual property.
  • Continuously evaluating the effectiveness of fiscal incentives.

    • Semicon 2.0 represents India's attempt to build a comprehensive and resilient semiconductor ecosystem covering design, manufacturing, packaging, R&D, materials and talent.

currentAffairs.Title: National Conference on Quantum Biotechnology
currentAffairs.Category: GS III - Science & Technology | Biotechnology | Quantum Technology
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: Explore the three key sessions of India’s Quantum Biotechnology Conference, covering quantum biology, academic research, biosensor translation, opportunities, challenges, and future pathways.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
National Conference on Quantum Biotechnology

Syllabus Areas:

GS III - Science & Technology | Biotechnology | Quantum Technology

The National Conference on Quantum Biotechnology brought together India’s quantum science and life-science communities to explore how quantum technologies can be translated into practical applications in diagnostics, biomedical imaging, drug discovery and precision medicine.

What is Quantum Biotechnology?

Quantum Biotechnology lies at the intersection of:

  • Quantum sensing
  • Quantum imaging
  • Quantum computing
  • Biotechnology and life sciences

    • It seeks to use the extraordinary measurement and computational capabilities of quantum technologies to address biological and medical questions that conventional instruments may not be able to answer.

    Major Focus of the Conference

    The conference focused on moving quantum biotechnology from lab research → industry → deployable healthcare technologies.

    It emphasised an interdisciplinary ecosystem bringing together physicists, biologists, clinicians, researchers, industry, start-ups and students to translate scientific innovations into practical healthcare solutions.

    Key Applications of Quantum Biotechnology

    A. Diagnostics: Quantum-grade sensing can potentially enable highly precise biological measurements, improving the detection and understanding of diseases.

    B. Biomedical Imaging: Quantum-enabled imaging technologies can offer new approaches to observing biological systems and processes.

    C. Drug Discovery: Quantum technologies can contribute to understanding complex biological and molecular interactions, potentially supporting more efficient drug-discovery processes.

    D. Precision Medicine: Quantum sensing and computing could support more precise understanding of biological characteristics, contributing to personalised healthcare approaches.

    E. Biosensing: A major focus is the development of quantum biosensors capable of detecting biological phenomena with remarkable precision.

    Major Challenges:

    The conference stressed that technological progress cannot occur through isolated efforts.

    Key challenges include:

    1. Interdisciplinary coordination: Quantum science and life sciences need to work together rather than operate in separate silos.

    2. Translation gap: A major challenge is converting promising laboratory demonstrations into deployable healthcare technologies.

    3. Industry participation: Greater participation from industry is required to convert research into commercially viable technologies.

    4. Start-up ecosystem: Start-ups need support to take emerging quantum-biotechnology solutions towards real-world applications.

    5. Talent development: India requires researchers and professionals capable of working across quantum science, biology, medicine and engineering.

    6. Manufacturing and testing capability: As technologies move towards clinical applications, India will need appropriate domestic manufacturing and testing capabilities.

    Why is Quantum Biotechnology Important for India?

  • Healthcare: Can potentially improve the precision of diagnostics, imaging, biosensing and precision medicine.
  • Scientific Research: Opens new avenues for studying biological questions beyond the capabilities of conventional instrumentation.
  • Innovation: Creates opportunities for new technologies and start-ups at the intersection of quantum science and biotechnology.
  • Strategic Technology Capability: Strengthens India's ability to develop advanced technologies domestically.
  • Industry: Can create new opportunities in quantum sensing, biosensors, medical technology and biotechnology.
  • Atmanirbhar Bharat: Building domestic manufacturing and testing capabilities can reduce dependence on external technologies and strengthen India's high-tech ecosystem.

    • Significance for the National Quantum Mission

    The conference reinforces an important shift in India's quantum strategy:

    From fundamental quantum research → towards application-driven quantum technology.

    The PIB release specifically highlights the objective of bringing quantum sensing, imaging, computing and biotechnology into a single platform, thereby positioning quantum-enabled life sciences as a priority area for India's research and healthcare innovation agenda.

currentAffairs.Title: Digital India BHASHINI: Building the Future of Language AI
currentAffairs.Category: GS II - Governance | GS III - Science and Technology , Artificial Intelligence
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: Explore how BHASHINI uses Language AI to promote multilingual digital inclusion, empower innovators, and strengthen India–Nepal cooperation in language technology and inclusive digital solutions.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Digital India BHASHINI: Building the Future of Language AI

Syllabus Areas:

GS II - Governance

GS III - Science and Technology , Artificial Intelligence

The Digital India BHASHINI Division (DIBD), under the Digital India Corporation (DIC), Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India, organised “BHASHINI शिल्पी” at the Embassy of India, Kathmandu, Nepal, on 31 August 2026.

The session brought together developers, technology practitioners and innovators from Nepal to explore how Language AI can be used to develop inclusive and multilingual digital solutions.

The “Innovate with BHASHINI” segment encouraged participants to share ideas and explore how BHASHINI could help transform problems into prototypes and scalable solutions.

Why Language AI Matters

  • Breaks language barriers in accessing digital services.
  • Uses AI-powered multilingual technology to make digital technology more inclusive, accessible and community-oriented.
  • Connects Artificial Intelligence with linguistic inclusion.

    • India–Nepal Language Technology Cooperation

  • BHASHINI शिल्पी strengthens India–Nepal cooperation in Language AI.
  • Brings together developers, academia and innovators.
  • Promotes knowledge exchange, idea sharing and co-creation.
  • Aims to build a cross-border ecosystem for inclusive digital solutions.

    • Significance for Digital Public Infrastructure

    BHASHINI represents an important dimension of India's digital transformation: language accessibility.

    Digital infrastructure becomes more inclusive when citizens can interact with technology in languages they understand.

    Therefore, Language AI can contribute to:

  • Reducing linguistic barriers
  • Improving accessibility of digital services
  • Enabling multilingual interfaces
  • Supporting technology adoption across communities
  • Creating opportunities for local developers and innovators

    • BHASHINI is India's national platform for AI-powered multilingual digital inclusion.

    Why is BHASHINI शिल्पी Important?

    1. From technology demonstration to technology creation: The programme does not merely showcase what Language AI can do. It encourages participants to build solutions themselves.

    2. Focus on real-world applications: Participants explore actual problem statements and use cases.

    3. Developer-centric approach: The programme provides developers and innovators with exposure to APIs and developer resources.

    4. Encourages scalability: The objective is not restricted to prototypes; participants are encouraged to think about scalable solutions.

    5. Promotes multilingual inclusion: Language technology can help make digital services accessible across linguistic communities.

    6. Strengthens India–Nepal cooperation: The programme creates a platform for technological collaboration between the two countries.

    BHASHINI uses Language AI to overcome linguistic barriers and make digital technology more inclusive. Its collaboration with Nepal can help build a stronger cross-border ecosystem for multilingual AI innovation.

currentAffairs.Title: Mission Zero: Depalpur Achieves Zero Legacy Waste
currentAffairs.Category: GS III - Environmental Pollution (Waste Management)
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: Depalpur becomes the first city under Swachh Shehar Jodi to achieve Zero Legacy Waste by remediating 1,250 MT of waste through scientific processing, recycling and community participation
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Mission Zero: Depalpur Achieves Zero Legacy Waste

Syllabus Areas:

GS III - Environmental Pollution (Waste Management)

Depalpur in Madhya Pradesh has achieved a significant milestone in urban waste management by becoming the first city under the Swachh Shehar Jodi initiative to achieve “Zero Legacy Waste.” The initiative resulted in the complete remediation of 1,250 metric tonnes of legacy waste that had accumulated over a period of five years.

The achievement demonstrates how inter-city collaboration, scientific waste management, source segregation, resource recovery and community participation can transform long-standing urban waste challenges into opportunities for environmental restoration and public welfare.

Depalpur’s Journey Towards “Zero Legacy Waste”

Depalpur's transformation was undertaken through cooperation between the Indore Municipal Corporation and Depalpur Nagar Parishad under the Swachh Shehar Jodi initiative.

Before focusing on the old dumpsite, Depalpur had established a waste-management system based on:

  • Door-to-door waste collection
  • Four-category waste segregation
  • 100% coverage of waste collection and segregation

    • Once this system was institutionalised, the focus shifted towards the challenge of clearing the accumulated legacy waste.

    Scientific Remediation of 1,250 Tonnes of Waste

    Under the initiative, Depalpur undertook the complete remediation of its dumpsite.

    The operation involved:

  • 1,250 metric tonnes of legacy waste
  • Waste accumulated over five years
  • More than 500 ragpickers from Indore Municipal Corporation
  • Dumpers
  • JCBs
  • Loaders

    • The waste was systematically segregated at the dumpsite into different streams so that each fraction could be directed towards its appropriate destination.

    This ensured that the operation was not merely a process of shifting waste from one location to another, but involved scientific processing and resource recovery.

    Resource Recovery from Legacy Waste

    The remediation process focused not only on removing waste but also on recovering useful resources.

  • 4.5 tonnes of recyclables — plastic, metal and glass — were recovered and sold to authorised recyclers.
  • 50–60 tonnes of Refuse Derived Fuel (RDF) was generated.
  • The RDF was taken to the NEPRA plant in Indore, shredded and sent to cement factories for co-processing.

    • What is Refuse Derived Fuel (RDF)?

    RDF is a fuel produced from the combustible portion of municipal solid waste after removing recyclable and unsuitable materials. It can be processed into a fuel suitable for use in industries such as cement manufacturing, reducing dependence on conventional fossil fuels.

    These initiatives illustrate a broader approach in which sanitation, environmental sustainability, heritage conservation and urban improvement are addressed together.

    Why Depalpur’s Model Matters

    The Depalpur experience offers several important lessons for urban governance.

    1. Peer Learning Can Accelerate Governance Outcomes: Instead of every city developing solutions independently, successful cities can share their experience and technical knowledge with other urban local bodies.

    2. Source Segregation is Fundamental: Four-category segregation and door-to-door collection created the foundation for effective waste processing.

    3. Waste Can Be a Resource: Recovery of recyclables and RDF shows how waste-management systems can incorporate resource recovery and recycling.

    4. Legacy Waste Requires Scientific Remediation: Old dumpsites cannot simply be shifted elsewhere. Scientific segregation, processing and authorised channelisation are essential.

    5. Citizen Participation Improves Sustainability: Community involvement can convert sanitation programmes from government-led projects into people-owned initiatives.

    6. Urban Land Can Be Reclaimed: Remediation can release previously degraded land for green spaces and community use.

    Way Forward

    The Depalpur experience suggests that tackling India's urban waste problem requires a combination of prevention, segregation, processing, recycling, scientific remediation and citizen participation.

    Urban local bodies can strengthen this approach by:

  • Ensuring universal door-to-door collection.
  • Promoting segregation at source.
  • Expanding scientific remediation of legacy dumpsites.
  • Strengthening recycling and resource recovery systems.
  • Building technical capacity of smaller urban local bodies.
  • Encouraging mentor–mentee partnerships between cities.
  • Involving citizens in maintaining reclaimed spaces.
  • Converting remediated dumpsites into environmentally productive public spaces.

    • Depalpur’s Mission Zero demonstrates integrated urban governance through mentorship, scientific remediation, segregation, resource recovery, restoration and community participation, transforming 1,250 MT of legacy waste into cleaner, greener public space.

currentAffairs.Title: PMJDY Challenges and Way Forward
currentAffairs.Category: GS III - Economy
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) was launched on 28 August 2014 by the Government of India. Read the Challenges and Way Forward
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
PMJDY Challenges and Way Forward

Syllabus Areas:

GS III - Economy

Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) was launched on 28 August 2014 by the Government of India. Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana is a financial inclusion initiative of the Government of India aimed at providing access to formal banking and financial services, particularly to underserved sections of society, thereby promoting financial security, inclusive growth and economic empowerment.

Read Why is it in News?

Challenges of PMJDY:

  • Opening accounts does not guarantee financial inclusion, especially when beneficiaries rarely use them for savings, payments, credit, insurance, or pensions.
  • Limited financial literacy prevents many first-time banking users from understanding interest rates, insurance, credit, digital banking procedures, and fraud prevention.
  • Digital exclusion persists because poor connectivity, limited smartphone access, inadequate digital skills, and accessibility barriers restrict participation in digital finance.
  • Insufficient banking infrastructure in remote areas makes access difficult when beneficiaries lack nearby branches, ATMs, banking correspondents, or reliable connectivity.
  • Banking Correspondents face operational challenges, including availability, reliability, transaction costs, and sustainability, potentially weakening last-mile delivery of financial services effectively.
  • Greater digital financial participation can increase exposure to phishing, OTP fraud, identity theft, fake banking calls, and fraudulent digital transactions.
  • Aadhaar authentication failures, incorrect beneficiary details, or technical problems can disrupt access to benefits, highlighting the need for grievance mechanisms.
  • Having a bank account does not automatically ensure affordable institutional credit, insurance, pensions, investments, or other essential formal financial services.
  • Women may possess Jan-Dhan accounts without achieving complete financial autonomy because social constraints, limited literacy, and restricted digital access persist.
  • Effective Direct Benefit Transfer requires accurate beneficiary identification, correct account linkage, successful transactions, and beneficiaries' ability to access transferred funds.

    • Way Forward:

  • Financial Literacy: Expand targeted awareness programmes to improve understanding of savings, credit, insurance, pensions, and digital banking.
  • Last-Mile Infrastructure: Strengthen banking correspondents, micro-ATMs, ATMs, and internet connectivity in underserved rural regions.
  • Active Usage: Encourage regular savings, digital transactions, and meaningful use of financial products.
  • Digital Inclusion: Provide affordable smartphones, reliable internet, vernacular interfaces, and digital-literacy training.
  • Cybersecurity: Strengthen fraud prevention, transaction monitoring, consumer awareness, and grievance redressal.
  • Institutional Credit: Improve access to affordable credit, insurance, pensions, and investments.
  • Women’s Empowerment: Promote women’s financial independence, literacy, entrepreneurship, and account usage.
  • Efficient DBT: Ensure reliable Aadhaar-linking, authentication, and transaction systems.
  • Inclusive Banking: Simplify procedures and provide multilingual, assisted services.
  • Outcome-Based Approach: Measure inclusion through usage, savings, credit, security, and empowerment.

    • PMJDY has transformed financial inclusion by bringing millions into the formal banking system. The next phase must move beyond account opening towards active usage, digital inclusion, financial security and empowerment, ensuring that every beneficiary gains sustainable economic opportunities and resilience.

currentAffairs.Title: Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana Completes 12 Years
currentAffairs.Category: GS III - Economy
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: PMJDY has transformed financial inclusion by expanding banking access, strengthening women and rural empowerment, enabling digital payments, and supporting direct benefit transfers for greater economic self-reliance.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana Completes 12 Years

Syllabus Areas:

GS III - Economy

The Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) has completed 12 years, marking a significant journey in India's efforts towards financial inclusion.

Union Minister for Women and Child Development Smt. Annpurna Devi described the scheme's journey as one that has moved “from financial inclusion to economic empowerment.”

What is PMJDY?

Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) was launched on 28 August 2014 by the Government of India. Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana is a financial inclusion initiative of the Government of India aimed at providing access to formal banking and financial services, particularly to underserved sections of society, thereby promoting financial security, inclusive growth and economic empowerment.

More than 59 crore Jan-Dhan accounts opened

A major achievement highlighted in the press release is the opening of more than 59 crore Jan-Dhan accounts.

These accounts have connected millions of citizens with the formal banking system and have contributed to building a foundation for greater financial self-reliance.

Women are major beneficiaries

Women account holders constitute a substantial share of the Jan-Dhan accounts.

  • 56% of Jan-Dhan accounts belong to women.

    • This highlights the important role of PMJDY in bringing women into the formal financial system and strengthening their access to banking services.

    Strong rural and small-town penetration

    The scheme has also achieved significant outreach beyond major urban centres.

  • 78% of Jan-Dhan accounts are in villages and small towns.

    • This demonstrates the scheme's focus on extending formal banking access to rural populations and people living in smaller settlements.

    Deposits cross ₹3.1 lakh crore

    The deposits held in Jan-Dhan accounts have crossed ₹3.1 lakh crore.

    This indicates the growing participation of account holders in the formal banking ecosystem and reflects the scale of financial resources brought into formal accounts through the scheme.

    Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)

    Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) is a Government of India mechanism through which government subsidies, welfare benefits, and financial assistance are transferred directly into beneficiaries’ bank accounts, reducing intermediaries and leakages.

    Example: A farmer eligible for a government income-support scheme receives the money directly in their bank account rather than through a middleman.

    Focus on women and rural families

    The Union Minister specifically highlighted the role of PMJDY in connecting citizens, particularly women and rural families, with the formal banking system.

    The broader significance is therefore not merely the creation of bank accounts, but the expansion of access to formal financial services among sections of the population that have traditionally faced greater barriers to banking access.

    Financial inclusion as a foundation for dignity and security

    The press release characterises the Jan-Dhan journey as more than simply opening bank accounts. It describes the scheme as a transformative journey of dignity, security and empowerment.

    It presents financial inclusion as an instrument that can strengthen people's economic participation and financial security.

    From financial inclusion to economic empowerment

    The central theme of the article is the evolution of PMJDY from a programme aimed at financial inclusion towards a broader foundation for economic empowerment.

    The Minister described the initiative as having laid a strong foundation for financial self-reliance, particularly among women and rural families.

    The key message can be understood through three stages:

    Financial Inclusion → Financial Access → Economic Empowerment

    Also Read Challenges and Way Forward

currentAffairs.Title: Micro-Irrigation for Sustainable Agriculture
currentAffairs.Category: GS III - Economy
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: Types of Micro-Irrigation under Per Drop - More Crop, Economic Survey 2020-21 data on PDMC.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Micro-Irrigation for Sustainable Agriculture

Syllabus Areas

GS III - Economy

Read Why is it in the News? Click Here

Types of Micro-Irrigation under PDMC

Impact Assessment Studies

Independent studies have highlighted the positive impact of the PDMC scheme. An evaluation by NITI Aayog during 2020-21 found the scheme aligned with national priorities. These include improving water use efficiency, increasing crop productivity, generating employment, and enhancing farmers' incomes. The study reported income gains ranging from 10% to 69%. Water use efficiency improved by 30%-70%. The scheme also created direct and indirect employment opportunities.

Significance for Indian Agriculture

PDMC is important because it connects water conservation with agricultural productivity and farmer income.

Its broader significance includes:

  • Promoting water-efficient agriculture.
  • Reducing dependence on inefficient irrigation practices.
  • Supporting groundwater-stressed regions.
  • Improving farm-level resource efficiency.
  • Encouraging modern irrigation technologies.
  • Reducing input costs.
  • Increasing crop productivity and farmer incomes.
  • Supporting horticulture and crop diversification.
  • Strengthening climate-resilient agriculture.
  • Contributing to sustainable food and nutritional security.

    • Per Drop More Crop (PDMC) has transformed India's irrigation approach by promoting efficient water use through micro irrigation technologies. The scheme has expanded access to modern irrigation while improving water use efficiency, crop productivity, and farmers' incomes.

    Supported by robust institutional mechanisms, digital implementation, and convergence with other government programmes, PDMC has strengthened sustainable irrigation practices nationwide. As India faces increasing pressure on its water resources, PDMC plays an important role in advancing resource-efficient, sustainable agriculture.

currentAffairs.Title: Water-Smart Farming with Per Drop More Crop
currentAffairs.Category: GS III - Economy
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: PDMC promotes micro-irrigation, efficient water use, higher productivity, reduced agricultural inputs, improved farmer incomes, groundwater conservation, and sustainable, climate-resilient agriculture across India.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Water-Smart Farming with Per Drop More Crop

Syllabus Areas:

GS III - Economy

Per Drop More Crop (PDMC) promotes micro-irrigation to enhance water-use efficiency and agricultural productivity. As of July 2026, it covers 115 lakh hectares. DBT and digital implementation improve transparency, while micro-irrigation delivers water savings, higher yields, lower costs, and increased farmers’ incomes.

Need for Efficient Irrigation in India

  • More than 80% of India's available water resources are used for agricultural irrigation.
  • At the same time, only around 50% of the net sown area has irrigation facilities.
  • This makes improvement in water-use efficiency a major national priority.
  • Micro-irrigation addresses this challenge by delivering water directly to crops while minimising losses.

    • PDMC under PM-RKVY

  • Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) was launched in 2007–08 for holistic development of agriculture and allied sectors.
  • It was restructured as Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (PM-RKVY) in October 2024.
  • PM-RKVY functions as an umbrella scheme merging nine schemes.
  • It covers areas such as:
  • Per Drop More Crop
  • Agricultural mechanisation
  • Soil health management
  • Crop diversification
  • Agri-startup accelerator fund
  • States have flexibility to reallocate funds between components according to their local agricultural requirements.
  • During 2025–26, ₹8,957.72 crore was released/sanctioned for PM-RKVY, including ₹3,226.36 crore for PDMC.

    • Benefits of Micro-Irrigation

  • Micro-irrigation enables efficient use of water by delivering it directly to the plant root zone, reducing wastage and improving irrigation efficiency.
  • It lowers the use of water, energy, fertilizers, and labour while supporting better crop growth and higher productivity through the precise application of water and nutrients.
  • The technology also encourages the cultivation of horticultural crops, improves cropping intensity, and brings marginal lands under productive use.
  • By reducing input costs and enhancing farm returns, micro-irrigation contributes to sustainable agriculture, strengthens farmers' livelihoods, and promotes long-term food and nutritional security.

    • New Flexibility for Water Conservation

    PDMC has introduced greater flexibility for states and UTs to undertake micro-level water storage and conservation activities.

    These include:

  • Diggis — large water storage tanks/farm ponds.
  • Water harvesting systems.
  • Individual as well as community-level water conservation structures.

    • These interventions aim to ensure reliable and sustainable water availability for micro-irrigation.

    Earlier, expenditure on such activities under the "Other Interventions" component was capped at:

  • 20% of allocation for general States/UTs.
  • 40% for North-Eastern States, Himalayan States and the UTs of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.

    • The revised guidelines allow States/UTs to exceed these limits according to their local requirements

    Also Read Types of Micro-Irrigation under PDMC

currentAffairs.Title: PARIVARTAN Scheme
currentAffairs.Category: GS III - Economy, Environment
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: PARIVARTAN Scheme accelerates replacement of old commercial vehicles with cleaner BS-VI and electric vehicles, offering financial incentives to reduce transport emissions and air pollution.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
PARIVARTAN Scheme

Syllabus Areas:

GS III - Economy, Environment

The PARIVARTAN (Programme for Accelerated Renewal and Incentivization of Vehicle Assets for Reducing Transport Air Pollution and Network Emissions) Scheme

  • The scheme was approved by the Union Cabinet on 3 June 2026.
  • It aims to accelerate the replacement of over 2 lakh old trucks and buses conforming to BS-IV or earlier emission norms.
  • The target vehicles are those registered in Delhi-NCR, including NCR districts of Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.
  • Replacement is encouraged with BS-VI or stricter-compliant diesel/CNG vehicles or electric vehicles (EVs).

    • Bharat Stage (BS) Norms:

    Bharat Stage (BS) norms are India’s vehicle-emission standards that regulate pollutants from automobiles, progressively requiring cleaner fuels and technologies to reduce air pollution and protect public health.

    Why is the scheme important?

    The scheme primarily seeks to:

  • Reduce transport-related air pollution.
  • Reduce vehicular emissions from older commercial vehicles.
  • Accelerate the transition towards cleaner and newer vehicles.
  • Encourage adoption of electric vehicles as an alternative to conventional diesel/CNG vehicles.
  • Support cleaner transportation in the highly polluted Delhi-NCR region.

    • Financial Outlay

  • Total financial outlay: ₹9,585 crore.
  • Central Government budgetary support: ₹5,041 crore.
  • Funding is provided through the National Capital Region Planning Board (NCRPB) under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA).
  • Implementation is being undertaken by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH).
  • OEMs are the vehicle manufacturers that produce the eligible new trucks, buses and other vehicles.

    • Launch and Current Progress

  • The PARIVARTAN Scheme was launched on 14 July 2026.
  • By 27 August 2026, more than 1,300 beneficiaries had registered on the PARIVARTAN Portal.
  • 42 banks and NBFCs have joined the initiative to provide interest subvention on vehicle loans.
  • 15 automobile OEMs have signed MoUs to provide discounts to eligible beneficiaries

    • PARIVARTAN is a targeted Delhi-NCR vehicle-renewal initiative that combines financial incentives, institutional financing and OEM participation to accelerate replacement of old commercial vehicles and reduce transport-related emissions.

currentAffairs.Title: Gnani Artha: India Launches Sovereign AI Stack with Evon 3.3 and Plexus
currentAffairs.Category: GS II - Governance | GS III - Science and Technology
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: India’s Gnani Artha launches a sovereign AI stack, strengthening indigenous AI capabilities, technological self-reliance, strategic autonomy, innovation, governance, and India’s global technological leadership.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Gnani Artha: India Launches Sovereign AI Stack with Evon 3.3 and Plexus

Syllabus Areas:

GS II - Governance

GS III - Science and Technology

Vice President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan launched ‘Gnani Artha’, described as a sovereign AI stack, at Uparashtrapati Bhavan, New Delhi. The platform combines Evon 3.3, a large language model, with Plexus, a platform designed to connect AI intelligence with real-world work and institutions.

The launch highlights India's growing emphasis on indigenous artificial intelligence capabilities, technological self-reliance and sovereign AI infrastructure.

What is ‘Gnani Artha’?

Gnani Artha is a sovereign AI stack developed by GNANI AI.

It brings together two key components:

Evon 3.3

  • A large language model (LLM).
  • Forms the AI intelligence component of the stack.
  • Represents India's effort to develop advanced AI technologies domestically.

    • Plexus

  • A platform that connects AI intelligence with real-world work and institutions.
  • It provides the practical/institutional layer through which AI capabilities can be applied.

    • In simple terms: Evon 3.3 = AI intelligence Plexus = application/institutional interface Gnani Artha = integrated sovereign AI stack

    What is a “Stack”?

    A stack means a group of technologies or tools that work together to perform a particular function.

    In the Gnani Artha article, “AI stack” means a combination of different AI technologies working together.

    What is a Sovereign AI Stack?

    The launch places significant emphasis on the concept of sovereign AI capabilities.

    A sovereign AI ecosystem aims to strengthen a country's ability to develop and deploy AI technologies using indigenous technological capabilities, rather than remaining dependent entirely on external technology providers.

    The Vice President stressed that India should develop its own technological capabilities and should not remain merely a consumer of technology.

    “We should not be consumers always; we need to create, so that others can consume.”

    This reflects the broader objective of moving India from being primarily a technology consumer to a technology creator and global technology leader.

    India’s Push for Technological Self-Reliance

    The launch was presented as an example of India's increasing technological capabilities.

    According to the Vice President:

  • India's technology ecosystem is becoming stronger.
  • Indian engineers are demonstrating the ability to work on frontier technologies.
  • India needs to build indigenous capabilities in strategic technologies.
  • Sovereign AI is important for strengthening India's technological and strategic autonomy.

    • The initiative therefore fits into the broader objective of technological self-reliance.

    AI as a Driver of Economic Growth

    The Vice President highlighted AI’s potential to transform the economy. Like the IT sector created jobs instead of eliminating them, AI can create new jobs, economic opportunities, innovation and growth, helping take India’s economic progress to the next stage.

    IndiaAI Mission & Centres of Excellence

  • IndiaAI Mission and AI Centres of Excellence aim to build a comprehensive ecosystem supporting artificial intelligence, research, innovation, and indigenous technology development.
  • These initiatives promote institutional AI applications and technological self-reliance, strengthening India's capacity to develop and deploy advanced technologies independently.

    • Strategic Importance of Sovereign AI

  • Sovereign AI strengthens India's technological autonomy, enabling independent technological choices aligned with national economic, security, administrative, and developmental priorities.
  • Indigenous AI capabilities can enhance economic competitiveness, national security, public administration, innovation, industrial development, and India's global technological leadership.

    • Why is Gnani Artha Important?

  • For India’s technology ecosystem: It demonstrates the ability of Indian technology companies and engineers to work on frontier AI technologies.
  • For strategic autonomy: Indigenous AI capabilities can reduce excessive dependence on external technological ecosystems.
  • For governance: AI can be integrated into government and parliamentary processes to improve accessibility and efficiency.
  • For linguistic inclusion: AI-based interpretation can make public institutions more accessible across India's diverse linguistic landscape.
  • For economic growth: AI can generate new avenues for employment, innovation and economic expansion.
  • For Viksit Bharat: Technological capability is positioned as an important component of India's development journey towards 2047.

    • UPSC Prelims 2026

    Q. Which of the following statements with regard to Large Language Models (LLMs) used in machine learning is/are correct?

  • LLMs assign probabilities to the next possible words and then pick the one with the highest probability.
  • LLMs process data through mathematical optimization to minimise prediction errors.
  • LLMs produce unbiased outputs.

    • Select the correct answer using the code given below:

    (a) 1 only (b) 1 and 2 only (c) 2 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3

    Answer: (b) 1 and 2 only

    Explanation

  • Statement 1 – Correct: LLMs use probabilities to predict the next possible token/word.
  • Statement 2 – Correct: During training, mathematical optimisation is used to reduce prediction errors.
  • Statement 3 – Incorrect: LLMs can produce biased outputs because their training data and design may contain biases.

currentAffairs.Title: Real Causes of Sugar Price Spike in India
currentAffairs.Category: GS III - Economy
currentAffairs.Short_Summary: India’s sugar price spike is driven by supply shortages and low stocks, but speculative hoarding and rising festival demand have significantly amplified the increase.
currentAffairs.Full_Content:
Real Causes of Sugar Price Spike in India

Syllabus Areas:

GS III - Economy

Retail sugar prices across India have witnessed a sharp increase, rising from around ₹45–₹48 per kg to ₹58–₹70 per kg. The price rise has raised concerns among policymakers and consumers, particularly ahead of the festival season.

While declining sugar production and weather-related supply constraints have contributed to the situation, speculative stockholding and hoarding by market intermediaries are the major catalysts behind the sharp retail price escalation.

The Reality is:
